title: Firecracker Beef and Brussels Sprouts Meal Prep

steps.text: Measure out enough dry rice for 3 3/4 cups (563 g) cooked.
steps.narration: You are aiming for 3 3/4 cups, or 563 grams, of cooked rice, which works out to somewhere between one and two cups dry.

detail.how: Different grains swell by different amounts, so start from the cooked weight you need and work backwards. One to two cups of dry rice will land you in range. Rounding up costs nothing, since spare rice becomes fried rice later in the week.
detail.watch_for: Guessing low. Coming up short on rice leaves the last container light.

steps.text: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, then cook it.
steps.narration: Wash the grains until the water coming off them is no longer cloudy, then set them cooking.

detail.how: Swirl the grains in cold water and drain, repeating until the runoff loses its milkiness. Rinsing away loose surface starch keeps the finished rice separate rather than gluey. A short or medium grain holds up best in the fridge over a week.
detail.watch_for: Skipping the rinse, which gives you a sticky mass by day three.

steps.text: Trim and halve 1 lb (454 g) of brussels sprouts.
steps.narration: Wash the vegetables, then cut the stem off each sprout and split it in half.

detail.how: Slice the dry woody base off each sprout and cut it lengthwise through the middle. Any outer leaves that look browned or gritty will loosen once the stem is gone, so pull those off and bin them. Frozen sprouts work here if fresh ones are awkward to get.
detail.watch_for: Leaving the stem attached. It stays tough no matter how long you cook it.

steps.text: Toss the sprouts with 1/2 tbsp (8 g) of oil, salt and pepper.
steps.narration: Put the halved sprouts in a big bowl, trickle over the oil, season, and turn them until every piece is coated.

steps.text: Air fry the sprouts in a single layer at 400F / 204C for 5 to 8 minutes.
steps.narration: Spread the sprouts across the air fryer basket in one layer and cook them at 400F, or 204C, for five to eight minutes.

detail.how: Lay them flat with cut sides down and no pieces stacked on top of each other, so hot air can reach every surface. Without an air fryer, spread them across a sheet pan and roast at the same temperature, allowing noticeably more time.
detail.watch_for: Overfilling the basket. Crowded sprouts release steam and go limp instead of browning.
detail.duration_hint: 5 to 8 minutes in an air fryer.

steps.text: Dice 4 stalks (20 g) of green onion tops for garnish.
steps.narration: Cut the green tops of four onion stalks into a small dice to scatter over the finished bowls.

steps.text: Dice the sweet onion and the poblano peppers small.
steps.narration: Cut one small sweet onion, about 100 grams, and two medium poblanos, about 200 grams, into a small dice.

detail.how: Halve the peppers, flatten them into strips, then cut across into pieces roughly the size of the onion dice so everything cooks at the same rate. Nearly all the heat sits in the seeds and pale inner ribs, so scrape those out for a mild dish or leave some in if you want warmth.
detail.watch_for: Poblanos are only slightly hotter than a green bell pepper, which substitutes fine if you cannot find them.

steps.text: Cut the lime into wedges, then cut each wedge in half.
steps.narration: Quarter the lime into wedges and halve each one so you have small pieces for topping.

steps.text: Pull the finished sprouts out and set them aside.
steps.narration: The sprouts should be done by now, so take the basket out and park it until later.

steps.text: Cook the onion and poblanos in a large skillet with oil and 1 tbsp (6 g) of red pepper flakes.
steps.narration: Heat a large pan over medium to medium-high, add a little oil, tip in the onion and peppers, and stir in a tablespoon of chilli flakes.

detail.how: The whole recipe is written around 1/2 tbsp, or 8 grams, of oil at this stage, so pour sparingly and only top up if the pan looks dry. Let the vegetables sit long enough between stirs to pick up some colour.
detail.watch_for: Drowning the pan in oil, which pushes the calorie count up for no flavour gain.

steps.text: Add 1 tbsp (15 g) of minced garlic to the middle of the pan.
steps.narration: Drop the garlic into the centre of the pan and let it cook down with the vegetables.

steps.text: Salt the vegetables, season the beef, then clear the centre and add 2 lb (908 g) of ground beef.
steps.narration: Give the vegetables a pinch of salt, season the beef with salt and pepper, sweep the vegetables out to the edge of the pan, and lay the beef in the gap.

detail.how: Salt on the vegetables draws their moisture out so they collapse rather than fry. Pushing them to the rim keeps the centre of the pan free and hot, which is where the beef needs to sit.
detail.watch_for: Seasoning nothing until the sauce goes in, which leaves the vegetables flat underneath it.

steps.text: Press the beef flat and let it brown before breaking it up.
steps.narration: Spread the beef so as much of it as possible touches the hot metal, and leave it alone until it colours.

detail.how: Maximum contact with the pan is what builds the browned crust. In an ideal world the beef would get its own pan rather than sharing with the vegetables, but sharing saves washing up at the cost of a little colour. If you want to cut the oil entirely, brown the beef first and cook the vegetables in its rendered fat afterwards.
detail.watch_for: Stirring immediately. Beef that never sits still weeps water and turns grey.

steps.text: Mix 5 tbsp (84 g) honey, 1/4 cup (60 g) hot sauce and 1 1/3 tbsp (20 g) apple cider vinegar.
steps.narration: While the beef browns, stir the honey, hot sauce and cider vinegar together until the honey dissolves.

steps.text: Whisk 1 1/2 tbsp (15 g) of cornstarch into the sauce.
steps.narration: Work the cornstarch into the sauce until it disappears.

detail.how: Slacken the cornstarch with a splash of cold water first, then stir that loose paste into the sauce. Dry starch dropped straight into liquid seizes into lumps that take forever to break down.
detail.watch_for: Lumps. They will dissolve with enough stirring, but it is slow and easy to avoid.

steps.text: Pour the sauce in once the beef is about 90 percent cooked, then add the sprouts.
steps.narration: When the beef is nearly done, stir the sauce again and pour it into the middle of the pan, then tip in the air-fried sprouts.

detail.how: Stir the sauce right before it goes in, because the starch settles to the bottom of the bowl within a minute or two. The residual heat finishes the last of the beef while the starch thickens.
detail.watch_for: Adding the sauce to raw beef. The water the meat still has to release will thin everything out.

steps.text: Stir everything together, thin with water if needed, and taste.
steps.narration: Fold it all together until the sauce coats the beef and the sprouts, loosen it with water if it has gone too thick, then taste.

detail.how: Keep folding until the glaze clings to the cut faces of the sprouts as well as the meat. If it has tightened past pouring, add water a small splash at a time.
detail.watch_for: Pouring in too much water at once. You can always add more, but there is no taking it back out.

steps.text: Spread 3/4 cup (112 g) of cooked rice into each of five containers.
steps.narration: Set out five meal prep containers and lay three quarters of a cup of rice across the base of each.

steps.text: Divide the beef and sprouts evenly between the five containers.
steps.narration: Share the beef and sprout mixture across the five containers on top of the rice.

detail.how: For portions that match to the gram, weigh the full pan, divide the total by five, and hit that number in each container. Scooping by eye gets close enough if all five meals are yours.
detail.watch_for: Heaping the first two containers and running thin on the last.

steps.text: Top each container with green onion and a lime wedge.
steps.narration: Finish every container with a scattering of green onion and one of the lime pieces.

steps.text: Swap in ground chicken, turkey or pork if you prefer.
steps.narration: Any ground meat works here, so use chicken, turkey or pork if beef is not what you want.

steps.text: Spoon off the rendered fat if you use a fattier grind.
steps.narration: Fattier beef is cheaper, but skim some of the fat out of the pan so the dish does not turn heavy.

detail.how: The 90/10 grind keeps the numbers at roughly 620 calories and 44 grams of protein per serving. With a fattier grind, tilt the pan and lift the pooled fat out with a spoon before the sauce goes in.
detail.watch_for: Leaving all the fat in with a heavy sauce, which makes the whole thing greasy.

steps.text: Cool the meals, lid them, and refrigerate for up to five days.
steps.narration: Let the containers come down close to room temperature before you put the lids on, then move them to the fridge.

detail.how: Lidding hot food traps steam, which condenses and waterlogs the rice underneath. Leave the containers open on the counter until they stop giving off heat, then seal and stack them.
detail.watch_for: Sealing them warm. They keep five days if you let them cool first.

steps.text: Reheat in the microwave, stirring every 30 seconds until hot through.
steps.narration: Tip a portion into a glass dish and microwave it, stirring every half minute until it is hot all the way through.

detail.how: There is no fixed time worth quoting, since it depends on your microwave and how cold the food is. Heat in short bursts, stir at each pause to even the temperature out, and test before you stop.
detail.watch_for: Blasting it in one long run, which overheats the edges and leaves the middle cold.

steps.text: Squeeze the lime over the top and mix before eating.
steps.narration: Squeeze the lime wedge over the beef and rice, stir it through, and eat.

title: Sheet Pan Protein Pancakes and Taco Mac

ingredients.name: salt
ingredients.unit: tsp (6 g) plus more to taste

steps.text: Pour 2 cups (480 g) of 2% milk into a blender.
steps.narration: Start the pancakes first so they bake while you cook everything else; put two cups of milk into a blender sitting on a scale.

detail.how: Weighing straight into the blender jug saves washing extra bowls and keeps the ratios exact. This quantity fills two half sheet pans, which cuts into 24 pieces.
detail.watch_for: Halve everything if you only want one tray.

steps.text: Add the applesauce, cottage cheese, maple syrup and vanilla, then blend smooth.
steps.narration: In go half a cup of applesauce, two and a half cups of cottage cheese, a quarter cup of maple syrup and a teaspoon of vanilla; run the blender until no curds remain.

detail.how: Blend longer than feels necessary. Cottage cheese curds that survive the blender show up as rubbery white specks in the baked sheet, and once the batter is mixed you cannot go back and fix them.
detail.watch_for: Stopping early. Rub a little between your fingers; it should feel completely smooth.

steps.text: Whisk 2 1/4 cups (540 g) of egg whites until frothy.
steps.narration: Beat the liquid egg whites in a separate bowl until they foam up and gain volume.

detail.how: You are not making meringue here, just working air in until the surface turns to bubbles and the volume noticeably climbs. That trapped air is what stops the baked sheet from turning dense.
detail.watch_for: Whisking a few token strokes. Keep going until the whites look genuinely foamy.

steps.text: Whisk the dry ingredients together until no clumps remain.
steps.narration: Combine six cups of oat flour, half a cup of powdered milk, a teaspoon of salt, four teaspoons of baking powder and a teaspoon of baking soda.

detail.how: Break up any lumps of flour or powdered milk now, while the mix is dry. Clumps that survive into the batter will not dissolve, and the raising agents need to be spread evenly or the sheet rises unevenly.
detail.watch_for: Leaving pockets of baking soda, which taste soapy in the finished pancake.

steps.text: Fold the blended mixture into the egg whites, then whisk in the dry ingredients.
steps.narration: Pour the blender contents into the frothy whites and combine them gently, then work the dry mix in slowly to make the batter.

detail.how: Move slowly and deliberately at this stage. Aggressive stirring knocks the air straight back out of the whites, and that air is doing the lifting. Add the dry mix in stages rather than all at once.
detail.watch_for: Beating it like a cake batter. Gentle folding keeps the volume you just built.

steps.text: Divide the batter between two lined sheet pans and bake at 375F / 190C for about 20 minutes.
steps.narration: Line two half sheet pans with parchment, spray them with oil, split the batter evenly between them, level the tops, and bake for around twenty minutes.

detail.how: Level the batter right to the corners with a spatula so the sheet bakes to an even thickness and cuts into equal pieces later. Parchment plus oil is worth the trouble, because this batter grips a bare pan.
detail.watch_for: Uneven depth, which leaves you with raw centres and overbaked edges.

steps.text: Chop a bunch (100 g) of green onions, keeping the whites and greens in separate piles.
steps.narration: Trim the stems from the onions and cut them up, holding back the green parts for garnish and setting the whites aside to cook.

steps.text: Dice two bell peppers (150 g each) to match the onion.
steps.narration: Take one green and one red pepper, cut off the top and bottom, pull out the seed core, and cut them into a small to medium dice.

detail.how: Match the pepper dice to the size of your onion pieces so the two soften at the same rate. Removing the whole seed capsule in one go is faster than picking seeds out afterwards.
detail.watch_for: Wildly mismatched sizes, which leave you with raw pepper next to collapsed onion.

steps.text: Heat a large pot with 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil and add 2 lb (908 g) of 93/7 ground beef.
steps.narration: Set a big pot over medium to medium-high heat, add the oil, and put the beef in.

steps.text: Season the beef with salt and pepper.
steps.narration: Season the beef to your taste with salt and pepper as it starts to cook.

detail.how: Extra lean beef is the right call here because the sauce it ends up in is rich enough to carry it. You get more protein for fewer calories without the meat tasting dry.
detail.watch_for: Under-seasoning at this stage. The spices come later and are not a substitute for salt.

steps.text: Let the beef brown, then break it up and stir in the onion whites and peppers.
steps.narration: Leave the beef undisturbed for a few minutes to colour, then break it apart and add the chopped vegetables.

detail.how: Use the waiting time to measure out the spice blend, since it goes in shortly after and you will not want to be reaching for jars mid-stir. Only break the beef up once it has had a chance to take on colour.
detail.watch_for: Chopping it up straight away, which stops it browning at all.

steps.text: Cook another 3 to 5 minutes, stirring about once a minute, until the peppers soften.
steps.narration: Let the beef finish and the vegetables soften, stirring roughly every minute so everything gets time against the heat.

steps.text: Stir in the chili powder, paprika, garlic powder, cumin and onion powder.
steps.narration: Once the beef has coloured, add two tablespoons of chilli powder, two teaspoons each of paprika, garlic powder and cumin, and a teaspoon of onion powder.

steps.text: Let the spices bloom for 1 to 2 minutes, then add the crushed tomatoes and beef broth.
steps.narration: Stir until the seasoning coats the meat and give it a minute or two before pouring in a can of crushed tomatoes and two cups of beef broth.

detail.how: A short spell against the hot pan draws the flavour out of ground spices, which is why the liquid waits. Keep it moving so nothing catches and burns on the bottom.
detail.watch_for: Adding the liquid immediately, which leaves the spices tasting raw and dusty.

steps.text: Stir in 10 oz (283 g) of dried macaroni and bring it to a light boil.
steps.narration: Tip the macaroni in and stir until it is spread through the pot, keeping as much of it as you can under the surface.

detail.how: Pasta only cooks where it is in contact with liquid, so push the noodles down into the sauce. A few pieces poking out above the line is fine, since steam under the lid takes care of those.
detail.watch_for: Leaving a raft of dry macaroni floating on top.

steps.text: Cover, drop the heat to low, and cook for 10 to 12 minutes.
steps.narration: Put the lid on, turn the heat right down, and leave it for ten to twelve minutes.

detail.how: At the eight minute mark, lift the lid and stir once. That stops anything sticking to the base and rotates the noodles from the top down into the liquid.
detail.watch_for: Cooking it hard. On a rolling boil the liquid disappears before the pasta is done.

steps.text: Test a noodle for doneness before you stop cooking.
steps.narration: Fish out a piece of macaroni whenever you stir and bite it to see whether it is ready.

detail.how: Gluten-free pasta needs closer watching than wheat pasta. It softens noticeably faster and will break down into mush if you leave it going past the point it is done.
detail.watch_for: Trusting the clock over the noodle, especially with gluten-free pasta.

steps.text: Turn off the heat and stir in 1 cup (240 g) of 2% milk.
steps.narration: Kill the heat and pour in a cup of milk, stirring it through the pot.

detail.how: The milk goes in only after the boiling has stopped. Dairy added to a pot that is still bubbling can split, leaving grainy specks through the sauce.
detail.watch_for: Adding the milk while it is still boiling.

steps.text: Taste and adjust with salt and pepper.
steps.narration: Have a taste and correct the seasoning until you are happy with it.

steps.text: Divide between five containers and top each with cheese and green onion.
steps.narration: Split the pot evenly across five containers, sprinkle three quarters of a cup, or 84 grams, of shredded cheese between them, and scatter the reserved green onion over the top.

detail.how: Five servings works out at roughly 674 calories and 54 grams of protein each. The cheese melts into the surface from the residual heat, and the green onion is there for colour and a bit of bite.
detail.watch_for: Adding the cheese to a stone-cold pot, where it just sits on top as dry shreds.

steps.text: Pull the pancake sheets from the oven and leave them to cool on the stovetop.
steps.narration: The pancake trays come out while the taco mac is cooking and sit on top of the oven to cool.

detail.how: If you want variety, press berries into the surface of one tray before it bakes and leave the other plain. Let both sheets cool fully in the pan before you try to cut them, or they tear.
detail.watch_for: Cutting them hot, which drags and shreds the surface.

steps.text: Lid the cooled taco mac containers and refrigerate for up to five days.
steps.narration: Once the meals have cooled and stopped steaming, put the lids on and move them into the fridge for the week.

detail.how: Steam trapped under a lid condenses and pools at the bottom, which turns the pasta slack. Wait until the containers feel close to room temperature before sealing them.
detail.watch_for: Sealing them warm. Cool first and they hold for five days.

steps.text: Reheat a portion for 2 to 3 minutes in the microwave, stirring about every minute.
steps.narration: At lunchtime, microwave a container for two or three minutes, stirring occasionally as it heats.

detail.how: Stirring at the pauses evens out the hot spots, which matters with a thick pasta dish that heats unevenly. If 93/7 beef is hard to find, ground chicken or turkey stands in fine.
detail.watch_for: One long unbroken blast, which scorches the edges and leaves the middle cold.

steps.text: Cut each pancake sheet into 12 slices, freeze them solid, then bag them.
steps.narration: Slice each tray into twelve pieces, spread them out in the freezer until firm, and move them into vacuum-seal bags.

detail.how: Freezing the pieces separately before bagging is what keeps them from fusing into one block. Lay them on a tray with a gap between each, wait until they are hard, then transfer them. Each plain slice is about 138 calories with 10.5 grams of protein.
detail.watch_for: Bagging them soft, which welds the whole batch together.

steps.text: Reheat the frozen pancakes in the microwave, or in an air fryer for crisp edges.
steps.narration: Microwave the slices until hot, or use an air fryer if you want the outside crisped up.

detail.how: Three slices come to just over 30 grams of protein, which makes a reasonable breakfast on its own. The microwave is quicker; the air fryer gives you a firmer, drier edge.
detail.watch_for: Reheating more than you will eat. They go back in the freezer poorly once thawed.

ingredients.name: salt
ingredients.unit: tsp (9 g) plus more to taste

steps.text: Rinse and cook 3 cups (450 g) of rice.
steps.narration: Wash the rice and get it cooking however you normally do it; you need three cups, about 450 grams, cooked.

detail.how: One cup of dry rice comes out at roughly two and a half to three cups cooked, so measure dry accordingly. Any cooking method is fine as long as it is going before you start on the chicken.
detail.watch_for: Starting the rice last. It is the one component that runs entirely unattended, so it should go first.

steps.text: Combine the smoked paprika, garlic powder and onion powder in a large bowl.
steps.narration: Into a big bowl go two teaspoons of smoked paprika, two teaspoons of garlic powder and a teaspoon of onion powder.

steps.text: Add the chili powder, salt, pepper, and 1 tbsp (15 g) each of lime juice, oil and water.
steps.narration: Add a teaspoon of chilli powder, one and a half teaspoons of salt, a teaspoon of pepper, then a tablespoon each of lime juice, oil and water to loosen it.

detail.how: The water is there purely to let the dry spices hydrate. Without a little liquid they sit as powder on the meat and scorch instead of sticking.
detail.watch_for: Leaving it dry. You want something spreadable, not dusty.

steps.text: Stir to a paste and coat 2 lb (908 g) of chicken thighs in it.
steps.narration: Mix until it forms a paste, then add the chicken thighs and turn them until every fold and surface is covered.

detail.how: Work the paste into the creases and the underside of each thigh with your hands rather than tossing them loosely. Thighs are the better cut for meal prep because their extra fat makes them very hard to dry out on a reheat.
detail.watch_for: Using breast instead. It overcooks easily and turns stringy after a few days in the fridge.

steps.text: Lay the chicken smooth side down on an oiled sheet tray.
steps.narration: Spray a large sheet tray lightly with oil and place the thighs on it with the smooth side facing the pan.

steps.text: Bake the chicken at 400F / 204C for 22 to 25 minutes.
steps.narration: Slide the tray into a 400F, or 204C, oven for about 22 to 25 minutes.

steps.text: Dice the sweet potato into 1/4 to 1/2 inch cubes.
steps.narration: Cut one medium sweet potato, about 12 ounces or 340 grams, into cubes between a quarter and half an inch across.

detail.how: Slice the potato into planks, then batons, then across into cubes. Keeping them a consistent size matters more than the exact measurement, because mismatched pieces mean some are mush while others are still hard.
detail.watch_for: Cutting them too big. Large cubes need much longer than the timings here allow.

steps.text: Cut 8 oz (227 g) of broccoli into small florets.
steps.narration: Break the broccoli down into small pieces, cutting from the stalk end upward through each floret.

detail.how: Turn each head upside down and cut up through the stalk into the crown rather than sawing across the top. Splitting the stem lets the florets fall apart cleanly instead of shattering into crumbs. Any stalk you keep should be chopped fine so it cooks in the same time as the tops.
detail.watch_for: Cutting horizontally through the florets, which showers the board with loose green dust.

steps.text: Roughly chop the green onions and toss the sweet potato with 1/2 tbsp (7.5 g) of oil.
steps.narration: Chop three or four green onions into rough pieces for the sauce, then coat the sweet potato cubes in half a tablespoon of oil.

steps.text: Salt the potatoes on an oiled sheet pan and roast at 400F / 204C for 10 to 15 minutes.
steps.narration: Spread the potato out on a lightly oiled sheet pan, season with salt, and roast for ten to fifteen minutes.

detail.how: Give the cubes room on the pan. This first stint only gets them part of the way there, since the broccoli joins them later and the two finish together.
detail.watch_for: Piling them into a heap, which steams them soft with no browned edges.

steps.text: Load a blender with the green onions, jalapeno, cilantro, garlic powder, cumin and a pinch of salt.
steps.narration: Into a blender or food processor go the chopped green onions, one small jalapeno, half a bunch of cilantro, a teaspoon of garlic powder, a quarter teaspoon of cumin and a pinch of salt.

detail.how: Tear the cilantro into shorter lengths before it goes in. Long intact stems wrap around the blade and stall the machine instead of getting chopped.
detail.watch_for: Dropping the bunch in whole and wondering why nothing moves.

steps.text: Add 2 tbsp (30 g) lime juice, 1 tbsp (15 g) oil and 1/2 cup (120 g) Greek yogurt, then blend.
steps.narration: Pour in the lime juice, oil and Greek yogurt, then run the machine until it comes together.

steps.text: Thin the sauce with water until it pours like a dressing.
steps.narration: Check the texture once it has broken down and add water, a tablespoon at a time, until it pours.

detail.how: You are after something loose enough to drizzle over a bowl but thick enough to cling. A single tablespoon of water is usually all it takes; add it, blend briefly, and look again.
detail.watch_for: Adding water in one go and ending up with a thin, watery pool.

steps.text: Toss the potatoes, push them to one side and coat the broccoli in 1/2 tbsp (7.5 g) of oil.
steps.narration: Pull the potato tray, turn the cubes over, shove them to one half of the pan, and toss the broccoli with oil in a bowl.

steps.text: Salt the broccoli, roast for another 10 to 12 minutes, and pull the chicken when it is done.
steps.narration: Spread the broccoli on the free half of the pan, salt it, and return the tray for another ten to twelve minutes; the chicken should be ready around the same time.

detail.how: Both trays are in the same oven, so keep an eye on the chicken while the vegetables finish. Set the chicken aside on its tray once it comes out and leave it alone.
detail.watch_for: Cutting the chicken straight away. Resting it keeps the juices in the meat instead of on the board.

steps.text: Divide the sauce evenly between five ramekins.
steps.narration: Portion the cilantro lime sauce into five small metal ramekins, one per meal.

steps.text: Chop the rested chicken into a medium to large dice and keep the juices from its tray.
steps.narration: Move the rested chicken to a board and cut it into chunks, saving whatever has rendered out onto the tray.

detail.how: Larger pieces hold moisture better through a week of reheating than fine shreds do. The fat and juice left on the sheet tray came off the chicken you already portioned, so it costs nothing extra to use.
detail.watch_for: Tipping the tray juices down the sink. That is free flavour for the broccoli.

steps.text: Pour the reserved chicken juices over the roasted broccoli.
steps.narration: Take the vegetable tray out once the potatoes are browned, and spoon the chicken juices over the broccoli.

steps.text: Mix the vegetables through, taste, and adjust with salt and pepper.
steps.narration: Turn everything together on the tray, taste a piece, and correct the seasoning.

steps.text: Divide the rice, vegetables, chicken and sauce between five containers.
steps.narration: Lay out five containers, split the rice between them, add a fifth of the potato, broccoli and chicken to each, and set a ramekin of sauce on top.

detail.how: Keeping the components separate looks tidier, but if you plan to stir it all together when you eat it, mixing now saves you a step later. Each serving lands at roughly 490 calories and 43 grams of protein.
detail.watch_for: Pouring the sauce over before storing. Yogurt sauce is better added at the table.

steps.text: Cool the meals, lid them, and refrigerate for up to five days.
steps.narration: Once the containers have cooled, put the lids on and move them to the fridge, where they will keep for five days.

detail.how: Wait until the food has stopped steaming before sealing, otherwise the trapped moisture drips back onto the rice. Glass containers store this better than plastic if you have them.
detail.watch_for: Lidding while hot, which leaves you with soggy rice by the second day.

steps.text: Set a blender jar on a kitchen scale.
steps.narration: Put the blender jar straight onto a scale so you can weigh everything into it.

detail.how: The whole wet base gets built inside the blender, so weighing into the jar itself means nothing extra to wash. Zero the scale between each addition rather than doing arithmetic in your head.
detail.watch_for: Forgetting to re-zero, which quietly throws off every ingredient after it.

steps.text: Add one 15 oz (425 g) can of unsweetened pumpkin, 1 cup (240 g) of 2% milk and 1 cup (227 g) of cottage cheese.
steps.narration: Weigh in the pumpkin, then the milk and the cottage cheese.

detail.how: Check the label and buy plain pumpkin puree, not the pre-sweetened pie filling, which already carries sugar and spice. The cottage cheese is standing in for heavy cream here, which is what keeps the protein high and the calories down. Fat-free cottage cheese works if you want to shave a little more.
detail.watch_for: Pie filling in a lookalike can. It will make the finished tray cloyingly sweet.

steps.text: Add 3 whole eggs, 1/2 cup (120 g) of maple syrup and 1/2 tsp (3 g) of salt.
steps.narration: Crack in three eggs, then add the maple syrup and the salt.

steps.text: Add 1 tsp (4 g) of baking powder and 1 tsp (4 g) of pumpkin pie spice.
steps.narration: Add the baking powder and the pumpkin pie spice.

detail.how: One teaspoon gives a gentle background warmth. If you want the tray to taste properly of cinnamon and clove, push the spice up by half again; there is nothing structural about the amount.
detail.watch_for: Old spice blends lose most of their punch. If the jar has been open a year, use more.

steps.text: Add 2 scoops (60 g) of vanilla protein powder.
steps.narration: Last into the jar goes the vanilla protein powder.

detail.how: Casein sets up slightly firmer and gives a marginally better crumb, but whey or a blend will bake fine. Use whatever is already in your cupboard rather than buying a second tub for one tray.
detail.watch_for: A strongly flavoured or heavily sweetened powder will dominate the pumpkin.

steps.text: Blend on high for about a minute until the mixture is completely smooth.
steps.narration: Lid on, blend for roughly a minute so everything comes together.

detail.how: The point of the blender is the cottage cheese: it has to break down until no curds are visible or you will find rubbery white specks in the baked slices. Run it longer than feels necessary and stop to scrape once if the top is not circulating.
detail.watch_for: Stopping while the mixture still looks flecked. It will not smooth out in the oven.

steps.text: Oil a 13x9 in casserole dish and tip in 3 cups (240 g) of rolled oats.
steps.narration: Spray the baking dish, then add the rolled oats straight into it.

detail.how: The oats stay whole on purpose so the finished tray keeps some chew. You can blend them in with the wet base instead if you prefer a uniform texture, but the batter thickens noticeably when you do.
detail.watch_for: A thin coat of oil on the corners and sides too, or the edge pieces will not lift out cleanly.

steps.text: Pour the pumpkin mixture over the oats and stir until evenly combined.
steps.narration: Pour the blended base over the oats and mix it all together right in the dish.

detail.how: Scrape the jar out with a spatula so none of the thick base is left clinging to the walls. Mixing directly in the casserole dish saves washing a separate bowl; just work gently so you do not splash batter over the rim.
detail.watch_for: Dry pockets of oats sitting in the corners. Drag the spatula along the base and the edges.

steps.text: Bake at 350F / 176C for 50 to 60 minutes, until the centre is set.
steps.narration: Into the oven at 350F / 176C for fifty minutes to an hour.

detail.how: Judge it by the middle, not the clock. Press the centre lightly with a fingertip; it should feel springy and stop jiggling as a liquid. The edges will always look done well before the middle does.
detail.watch_for: Pulling it out at fifty minutes on faith. An underbaked centre will collapse into wet oats when you cut it.

steps.text: Stir together 1/2 cup (100 g) Greek yogurt, 1/2 cup (100 g) whipped cream cheese and 2 tbsp (30 g) maple syrup until smooth.
steps.narration: While it bakes, make the frosting from yogurt, whipped cream cheese and maple syrup.

detail.how: This is a lighter stand-in for a real cream cheese frosting, built on three ingredients and no butter or icing sugar. Beat it until there are no lumps of cream cheese left; the whipped kind starts soft and gives in quickly.
detail.watch_for: Fridge-cold cream cheese stays lumpy. Let it sit out for a few minutes first.

steps.text: Transfer the frosting to a zip-top bag and chill it until the oatmeal is ready.
steps.narration: Scrape the frosting into a plastic bag and keep it in the fridge.

steps.text: Cool the tray to near room temperature, run a flexible spatula around the edges, and cut it into six slices.
steps.narration: Let the tray cool on the counter, free the edges with a spatula, then cut six equal pieces.

detail.how: Leave it on the counter until it is barely warm. A hot tray tears when you cut it; a cooled one has firmed up enough to hold clean edges. Trace a thin bendy spatula all the way around the perimeter first so the slab releases from the sides before you divide it.
detail.watch_for: Cutting while hot. The slices will slump and smear rather than lift out square.

steps.text: Lift each slice into a meal prep container and pipe the frosting over the top.
steps.narration: Slide the spatula under each piece, move it to a container, and pipe frosting across it.

detail.how: Snip a small corner off the chilled bag and draw lines across each slice. Piping is purely cosmetic; spooning it over and spreading it works exactly as well.
detail.watch_for: Cutting too big a hole in the bag, which dumps the frosting in one blob.

steps.text: Or keep the frosting in a separate tub and add it after reheating.
steps.narration: You can also store the frosting on its own and spoon it on once the oatmeal is hot.

detail.how: Frosting added after the microwave stays cool and thick against the warm oatmeal, which is the better eat. Frosting it in advance is the move only if you are carrying these to work or school and want one container instead of two.
detail.watch_for: Nothing goes wrong if you microwave the frosting with the slice; it just loosens and soaks in.

steps.text: Refrigerate the containers and eat them within five days.
steps.narration: Store them in the fridge and plan to finish them inside five days.

steps.text: Handle the sixth serving by doubling up one day, freezing it, or sharing it.
steps.narration: Six slices over five days means one extra, so eat two one day, freeze it, or give it away.

detail.how: The tray makes six but the five-day rule leaves one spare. Eating two on a single day is simplest; wrapping one and freezing it also works, as does handing it to a housemate. Six days in the fridge is still perfectly edible if you would rather not bother.
detail.watch_for: Letting the last piece drift to day seven at the back of the shelf.

title: Sausage, Egg and Cheese Savory Baked Oatmeal

steps.text: Set a large bowl on a scale and add 1 tsp (6 g) of salt to start the sausage seasoning.
steps.narration: You are making your own breakfast sausage, so start a seasoning mix in a big bowl on a scale.

detail.how: The spice blend goes into the bowl before the meat, so it can be broken up and evenly mixed on its own. Ground pork is the choice here for fat and flavour, but ground turkey is the next best swap and any ground meat will work.
detail.watch_for: Trying to mix dry spices into the raw meat directly. Clumps end up in some bites and nothing in others.

steps.text: Add 1 tsp (3 g) each of garlic powder, onion powder, cayenne, paprika and black pepper, then 1 tsp (1 g) dried oregano, 1 1/2 tsp (2 g) rubbed sage and 1 tbsp (12 g) brown sugar.
steps.narration: Weigh in the rest of the spices along with the sage and the brown sugar.

detail.how: Sage is the flavour that makes this read as breakfast sausage rather than generic seasoned pork, so do not leave it out. The brown sugar balances the salt and cayenne and helps the meat caramelise in the pan.
detail.watch_for: Cayenne is the one to adjust. A full teaspoon carries real heat across six servings.

steps.text: Break up the sugar lumps, mix the spices together, then add 1 lb (454 g) of 90/10 ground pork.
steps.narration: Work the clumps out of the brown sugar, stir the blend even, then add the pork.

steps.text: Mix the seasoning through the pork by hand, then dice one green bell pepper (150 g) small.
steps.narration: Get your hands in and toss the pork until the seasoning is spread through, then start on the vegetables.

detail.how: Hands beat a spoon here because you can feel where the seasoning is still concentrated. Toss and fold rather than kneading; overworking ground pork makes the cooked pieces dense and springy.
detail.watch_for: Under-mixing. Every bite of the finished tray should taste seasoned, not just some of them.

steps.text: Dice one small onion (100 g) to the same size as the peppers.
steps.narration: Cut the onion to match the pepper so both cook at the same rate.

detail.how: Half a medium onion works if you do not have a small one. Matching the two dice sizes matters more than the exact size you pick, since mismatched pieces finish at different times in the pan. Kale or spinach can go in alongside if you want more vegetables in the tray.
detail.watch_for: Cutting the onion larger than the pepper. It will still be raw and sharp when the pepper is soft.

steps.text: Heat a skillet over medium-high with 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil, lay the pork in flat, and let it sit for a minute or two.
steps.narration: Get the pan hot, press the sausage mixture out across it, and leave it alone to colour.

detail.how: Spread the meat into a thin even slab so as much of it as possible is in contact with the hot metal. Leaving it undisturbed is what builds the browned crust; stirring immediately just steams it grey.
detail.watch_for: The brown sugar in the mix scorches faster than plain meat would, so do not walk away from the pan.
detail.duration_hint: 1 to 2 minutes on the first side.

steps.text: Flip the slab, break it into small pieces, and cook until the pork is done through and caramelised.
steps.narration: Turn it over, break it up, and finish cooking until the pieces are deeply coloured.

detail.how: Once the first face has colour, flip it in sections and then chop it down with the edge of your spatula. Keep the pieces small enough that they distribute through the oat base rather than sitting as lumps.
detail.watch_for: Pieces that look grey rather than caramelised. Give them more time in contact with the pan.

steps.text: Move the sausage to a plate, add another 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil, then add the peppers and onions with a pinch of salt.
steps.narration: Take the pork out, oil the pan again, and tip in the peppers and onions with a little salt.

steps.text: Cook the vegetables 3 to 5 minutes, take the pan off the heat to cool, then beat 2 eggs smooth in a large bowl on a scale.
steps.narration: Give the vegetables a few minutes to colour, set them aside to cool, and start the oat base with two beaten eggs.

detail.how: You want visible browning on the pepper and onion, not just softness; that colour is most of the flavour they contribute. Cooling them off the heat matters because hot vegetables would start to set the eggs when they meet the base.
detail.watch_for: Adding scorching-hot vegetables to the egg mixture and getting scrambled bits through it.

steps.text: Add 2 cups (480 g) of 2% milk and 1 cup (227 g) of cottage cheese to the eggs and stir.
steps.narration: Pour the milk in with the cottage cheese and give it a stir.

steps.text: Add 3 cups (240 g) of rolled oats, 1/2 cup (60 g) of oat flour, 1 tsp (4 g) of baking powder and 1/2 tsp (3 g) of salt.
steps.narration: Now the dry side: oats, oat flour, baking powder and salt.

detail.how: The flour is doing structural work, binding the tray so slices hold together instead of crumbling. Plain all-purpose flour substitutes for the oat flour with no change in method.
detail.watch_for: Skipping the flour to save carbs. The tray will not slice cleanly without it.

steps.text: Stir until the oats and flour are hydrated, then fold in the sausage, the peppers and onions, and 1 cup (112 g) of shredded cheddar.
steps.narration: Mix wet into dry until no flour is loose, then add the sausage, vegetables and cheddar.

detail.how: Keep stirring until you see no dry flour and the oats have visibly drunk up liquid; that hydration is what stops a gritty texture. Only then add the solids, so you are not fighting a full bowl to combine the base.
detail.watch_for: Pockets of dry flour hiding at the bottom of the bowl.

steps.text: Give the bowl one more thorough mix, then oil a 13x9 casserole dish, sides included.
steps.narration: Mix everything through one last time and grease the baking dish well.

detail.how: Spray the dish and then wipe the oil up the walls with a paper towel so the corners and sides are coated too. That is where a savoury tray with cheese in it most often welds itself to the pan.
detail.watch_for: Oiling only the flat bottom. The edge slices will tear coming out.

steps.text: Spread the mixture level in the dish and bake at 375F / 190C for 40 to 45 minutes, until set in the centre.
steps.narration: Tip it into the middle of the pan, level it out, and bake at 375F / 190C for forty to forty-five minutes.

detail.how: Push the mixture right into the corners and flatten the surface with a spatula. An uneven surface bakes unevenly, leaving one end dry while the thick end is still loose. Test the middle for set rather than trusting the timer.
detail.watch_for: A domed middle. It will still be wet when the thin edges are overcooked.

steps.text: Check it at 30 minutes and tent it with foil for the last 10 to 15 minutes if the top is colouring too fast.
steps.narration: Look in at the thirty minute mark and cover it with foil if the surface is getting dark.

detail.how: It bakes uncovered by default, but ovens vary enough that the cheese on top can be dark well before the centre is set. Foil laid loosely over the top stops the browning without stopping the bake. Chopped parsley over the finished tray is purely for looks.
detail.watch_for: Sealing the foil tightly to the rim, which traps steam and softens the surface.

steps.text: Cool the tray, run a knife around the perimeter, and cut it into six pieces.
steps.narration: Let it cool on the counter, free the edges with a knife, then cut six slices.

detail.how: Cut once down the middle of the long side, turn the pan a quarter turn, and make two more cuts across to give thirds. That gets you six even pieces with three cuts and no measuring.
detail.watch_for: Cutting a hot tray. Wait until it is barely warm or the slices slump.

steps.text: Plan to eat them within five days.
steps.narration: Keep them no longer than five days in the fridge.

steps.text: For the odd sixth serving, cut five larger pieces instead, double up one day, or freeze one.
steps.narration: Six slices across five days leaves one over, so cut five instead, eat two one day, or freeze it.

detail.how: Six days in the fridge is almost certainly fine if you would rather not think about it. If that bothers you, cut into five larger portions from the start so the maths works out, or take one as a late-night snack.
detail.watch_for: Freezing works but the texture softens slightly on thawing.

steps.text: Let the portions finish steaming, lid them, and refrigerate for the week.
steps.narration: Wait until they stop steaming, put the lids on, and move them to the fridge.

detail.how: Leave the containers open until no visible steam is coming off. Sealing warm portions traps condensation on the lid, which drips back down and makes the top of the slice soggy by day two.
detail.watch_for: Lidding them early to get the kitchen tidied up. That is what ruins the texture.

ingredients.name: cooked day-old rice
ingredients.unit: cups (450 g), from about 200 g dry

ingredients.name: salt
ingredients.unit: tsp (6 g), plus more to taste

steps.text: Cook the rice the night before and chill it in the fridge.
steps.narration: Start a day ahead: cook the rice and refrigerate it overnight.

detail.how: A night in the fridge dries the surface of the grains out, and dry grains fry rather than steam. Spread it in a shallow layer so it cools quickly and does not clump into one solid block.
detail.watch_for: Using rice cooked an hour ago. It is still wet inside and turns the pan gluey.

steps.text: Measure out 3 cups (450 g) of cooked rice and take out one medium red bell pepper (150 g).
steps.narration: You need three cups of cooked rice, which is about 200 g dry. Then start on the vegetables with the pepper.

steps.text: Seed the pepper and cut it into thin strips, then dice one zucchini (150 g) medium.
steps.narration: Take the seeds out of the pepper and slice it thin, then cut the zucchini into a medium dice.

detail.how: For the zucchini, split it lengthways a few times to make long planks, cut those into strips, then cut across the strips to get cubes. Keep the pieces on the larger side so they still have bite after the pan and the microwave.
detail.watch_for: A fine dice on the zucchini. It turns to mush by the time you reheat the meal.

steps.text: Cut one medium onion (200 g) into thin strips and mince 3 to 4 cloves of garlic to 1 tbsp (15 g).
steps.narration: Slice the onion thin to match the peppers, then mince the garlic.

steps.text: In a bowl on a scale, combine 1 tbsp (15 g) oil, 1 tbsp (15 g) lemon juice, 2 tbsp (30 g) Greek yogurt, 2 tsp (6 g) garlic powder and 2 tsp (6 g) curry powder.
steps.narration: Build the marinade: oil, lemon juice and yogurt, then the garlic powder and curry powder.

detail.how: The yogurt is the body of this marinade. Its acidity and its thickness let the spices cling to the chicken instead of sliding off, and the lemon juice sharpens it. Oil carries the fat-soluble flavour out of the curry powder.
detail.watch_for: Using flavoured or sweetened yogurt. It needs to be plain.

steps.text: Add 1 tsp (3 g) each of paprika, coriander and cumin plus 1 tsp (6 g) of salt, and stir until no clumps remain.
steps.narration: Add the rest of the spices and the salt, then stir the marinade smooth.

detail.how: Stir hard enough that the powders disappear into the yogurt completely. Any dry pocket left in the bowl becomes a bitter concentrated patch on one piece of chicken.
detail.watch_for: Streaks of unmixed spice sitting on the surface.

steps.text: Cut 2 lb (908 g) of boneless skinless chicken thighs into thin strips about 1/4 in thick, trimming fat and gristle.
steps.narration: Slice the chicken thighs into quarter-inch strips, cutting away any fat or gristle as you go.

detail.how: Thighs stay juicy where breast would dry out at this thickness. Slice against the grain and keep the strips uniform so they all finish at the same moment. Trim the pale gristle and the loose fat now; it will not render out in a fast sear.
detail.watch_for: Thick uneven pieces. The thin ones overcook while you wait on the thick ones.

steps.text: Toss the chicken through the marinade by hand until every piece is coated.
steps.narration: Get your hands in the bowl and turn the chicken until it is fully coated.

detail.how: Thin strips give you a lot more surface for the marinade to grab, which is most of why they are cut this way rather than cubed. Work from the bottom of the bowl upward so the pieces underneath get their share.
detail.watch_for: Pieces stuck together in a stack, with bare patches under them.

steps.text: Rest the chicken in the fridge for 30 minutes, or go straight to the pan.
steps.narration: You can chill it for half an hour to deepen the flavour, or just cook it now.

detail.how: Thirty minutes in the fridge lets the salt and acid work a little further into the surface. The gain is real but small, and skipping it costs you very little in the finished bowl.
detail.watch_for: Marinating far longer than that. Lemon and yogurt will start to break the texture down.

steps.text: Add a splash of oil to a pan and cook about a third of the chicken at a time.
steps.narration: Cook the chicken in three batches so the pan stays hot.

detail.how: Budget an extra 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil in total across the batches. Three loads is the right split for two pounds in a standard skillet; you want every strip touching metal with space around it.
detail.watch_for: Tipping the whole bowl in to save time. That is what turns a sear into a boil.

steps.text: Use about a teaspoon of oil per batch and cook over medium-high, letting the colour build before you shake the pan.
steps.narration: A teaspoon of oil before each batch, medium-high heat, and leave it still until it colours.

detail.how: Thin strips cook through very fast, so the browning is the limiting factor, not doneness. Let each piece sit until the underside has taken colour, then toss the pan once and give the other face the same.
detail.watch_for: Constant stirring. It never lets any surface get hot enough to brown.

steps.text: Move each finished batch to a plate and carry on until all the chicken is cooked.
steps.narration: Take each batch out to a plate and repeat until the bowl is empty.

detail.how: Space in the pan lets the water the chicken releases evaporate instead of pooling. That is what keeps the surface above the temperature where browning reactions happen. A crowded pan traps the water, the temperature drops, and the meat goes pale and grey.
detail.watch_for: Liquid gathering in the pan. If you see it, the batch is too big.

steps.text: In the same pan add 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil with the peppers and onions, season lightly with salt, and cook 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.narration: Straight into the same pan with the peppers and onions and another spoon of oil.

detail.how: Do not wash the pan. The browned scraps left from the chicken lift into the vegetables as they release moisture, and that is free flavour. A pinch of salt now draws water out and helps them soften.
detail.watch_for: Burnt rather than browned residue. If the pan scorched during the chicken, wipe it out first.

steps.text: Add the zucchini and toss until it just begins to soften.
steps.narration: Now the zucchini goes in, just long enough to take the raw edge off.

detail.how: Stop while the pieces still have structure. Reheating in the microwave is a second round of cooking, so anything fully soft now will be watery and collapsed when you actually eat it on Wednesday.
detail.watch_for: Cooking to the texture you want on the plate. Aim short of it.

steps.text: Stir in the garlic until fragrant, then add 1 tbsp (15 g) of tomato paste and coat everything.
steps.narration: Garlic goes in late so it does not burn, then the tomato paste.

detail.how: Garlic is held back until this point deliberately: it scorches and turns bitter in a minute over high heat. Stir it just until you can smell it, then get the tomato paste in and spread it through the vegetables.
detail.watch_for: Brown flecks of garlic. Once it burns you cannot rescue the pan.

steps.text: Cook the paste for about 2 minutes, then add the 3 cups (450 g) of cooked rice.
steps.narration: Give the tomato paste a couple of minutes to cook out, then tip the rice in.

detail.how: Raw tomato paste tastes tinny and sharp. Two minutes in a hot pan darkens it and turns it savoury and deep. If the pan looks dry once the rice hits it, another 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil is fine.
detail.watch_for: Adding rice to raw paste. That tinny edge stays in the finished dish.

steps.text: Break up the rice clumps and colour it through, then return the chicken and toss to combine.
steps.narration: Work the rice apart and let it take on colour before the chicken goes back in.

detail.how: Do the clump-breaking before the chicken joins the pan. Once two pounds of meat are in there the pan is full and you cannot move anything without spilling it over the sides.
detail.watch_for: Cold lumps of rice hiding in the middle of the pan.

steps.text: Taste, adjust with salt and pepper, and divide between five meal prep containers.
steps.narration: Taste it, correct the seasoning, then split it across five containers.

steps.text: Garnish each portion with chopped cilantro if you like.
steps.narration: A little chopped cilantro on top adds colour and freshness, but it is optional.

steps.text: Let the containers stop steaming, put the lids on, and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Wait until the steam has died off, lid them, and store them in the fridge for the week.

detail.how: Sealing a hot container traps steam that condenses on the lid and rains back onto the rice, softening it over the week. Leave them open on the counter until they are near room temperature first.
detail.watch_for: Water pooled on the underside of the lid the next morning. That is a sign you closed them too early.

steps.text: For larger meals, split the pan into three or four servings instead of five.
steps.narration: If you are not counting calories, divide it into three or four portions rather than five.

detail.how: Five portions is what keeps each meal under about 491 calories with 40 g of protein. Splitting into four or three simply scales those numbers up and gives you a fuller plate.
detail.watch_for: Nothing changes in the cooking, only the division at the end.

title: Gluten-Free Chocolate Chip Cookie Bread Bites

ingredients.name: rolled oats, certified gluten-free (blended into flour)

steps.text: Pick out oats that are labeled gluten-free.
steps.narration: Start with oats, and check the label if gluten matters to you.

detail.how: Oats are naturally free of gluten, but many brands run through mills that also handle wheat, so cross-contact is common. Only a bag that carries a gluten-free claim on the packaging has been kept separate. Warehouse-club bags are the cheapest way to buy them by weight.
detail.watch_for: Assuming any oat is safe. Without the label there is no guarantee the batch stayed clear of wheat.

steps.text: Blend the oats into a fine flour.
steps.narration: Run the oats through a blender until they turn into powder.

detail.how: Tip the dry oats into a blender jar and run it until nothing gritty is left and the texture reads as powder rather than broken flakes. Doing this at home costs a fraction of buying bagged oat flour. Make extra and keep it in a sealed jar so the blender stays in the cupboard next time.
detail.watch_for: Stopping while flat flakes are still visible. Coarse meal soaks up liquid unevenly and leaves the dough wet.

steps.text: Mix the oat flour, salt and baking soda in a large bowl.
steps.narration: Weigh 320 g of oat flour into a big bowl with 4 g of salt and 8 g of baking soda, and stir.

detail.how: Set the bowl on a scale and zero it between additions: 2 2/3 cups or 320 g of oat flour, 1 tsp or 4 g of salt, 2 tsp or 8 g of baking soda. Stir with a whisk or fork until the colour is uniform.
detail.watch_for: Clumps of oat flour. They hide dry pockets that never hydrate and show up as chalky bites later.

steps.text: Beat four eggs in a second bowl, then whisk in the Greek yogurt.
steps.narration: Crack four eggs into another bowl, beat them smooth, then add 600 g of Greek yogurt.

detail.how: Work the eggs with a whisk or a fork until the yolks and whites are one colour with no ropey streaks left, then fold in 2 2/3 cups or 600 g of yogurt. Full-fat gives a richer mouthfeel; non-fat works and trims the calories.
detail.watch_for: Adding the yogurt before the eggs are broken up. Loose yolk pockets are much harder to chase out once the yogurt is in.

steps.text: Add the sugar to the wet bowl.
steps.narration: Weigh in 3 tbsp or 40 g of sugar.

detail.how: Plain sugar at 40 g is the baseline. A non-nutritive sweetener such as monk fruit, sucralose or stevia can stand in, but use only half the weight, so 20 g, because they taste sweeter spoon for spoon. Maple syrup swaps in at the same 40 g.
detail.watch_for: Matching a sweetener gram for gram against sugar, which makes the batch cloying.

steps.text: Add the vanilla extract and the first half cup of chocolate chips.
steps.narration: Pour in 16 g of vanilla and 120 g of chocolate chips.

steps.text: Stir the wet mixture, then fold it into the dry ingredients to form a dough.
steps.narration: Mix the wet bowl until it is even, then combine it with the dry bowl.

detail.how: Stir the yogurt, eggs, sugar and vanilla until you cannot see separate layers, then tip that into the flour bowl. Push through it firmly and steadily until the whole thing pulls together as one mass with no dry flour clinging to the sides.
detail.watch_for: A timid stir. This batter is thick, so it needs real pressure before it comes together.

steps.text: Rest the dough for 5 minutes while you oil one or two sheet trays.
steps.narration: Leave the dough on the counter for about 5 minutes and spray your trays in the meantime.

detail.how: The rest gives the oat flour time to drink up the liquid, which firms the dough and keeps the scoops from spreading flat. Use those minutes to coat one or two large sheet pans with oil spray.
detail.watch_for: Scooping straight away onto a bare pan. The dough is slacker than it will be in five minutes, and unoiled pans grip hard.

steps.text: Scoop 1 oz (30 g) portions onto the trays, 1 to 2 inches apart.
steps.narration: Use a 30 g cookie scoop and leave an inch or two between each piece.

detail.how: A 1 oz cookie scoop keeps every piece the same size, which matters when you are counting calories per piece and when they all need the same bake time. This batch yielded 53 pieces across two pans. Halve everything if you are not stocking the freezer.
detail.watch_for: Crowding the pan. These spread a little, and touching pieces bake into one slab.

steps.text: Press two or three chocolate chips onto the top of each piece.
steps.narration: Take the reserved 60 g of chips and dot two or three onto every scoop.

detail.how: Holding back 1/4 cup or 60 g for the tops guarantees visible chocolate on every single piece rather than leaving it to chance in the mix. Push each chip in lightly so it does not roll off in the oven.
detail.watch_for: Dumping all the chips into the dough. Some pieces end up with none at all.

steps.text: Add another 60 g of chocolate chips if you want them sweeter.
steps.narration: For a richer result, work in an extra 60 g of chips.

steps.text: Bake at 375F / 190C for 15 to 20 minutes.
steps.narration: Into a 375F / 190C oven for 15 to 20 minutes.

detail.how: One tray alone finishes nearer the 15 minute mark. Two trays in together slow the oven down and can take the full 20. Check them from 15 minutes on rather than trusting the timer.
detail.watch_for: Letting the tops go dark. Once they brown deeply they dry out, so pull them the moment the colour is right.

steps.text: Cool on the pan for a few minutes, then lift them off with a spatula.
steps.narration: Let them sit on the counter briefly, then release them with a spatula.

detail.how: A few minutes of resting lets the crumb set so the pieces hold together when you slide a thin spatula underneath. Each one lands around 53 calories, 7.3 g carbs, 2.4 g protein and 1.6 g fat.
detail.watch_for: Prying them off hot. They tear while the inside is still soft.

steps.text: Eat them warm, straight from the oven or after a short spell in the microwave.
steps.narration: These are at their best warm, so heat them if they have cooled.

steps.text: Flash freeze any extras on the tray so they set solid before packing.
steps.narration: Freeze the leftovers spread out on the pan before you bag them.

detail.how: Freezing them loose and uncovered firms the chocolate and chills the crumb all the way through. Skip this and vacuum sealing will smear melted chocolate everywhere and squash the pieces into one frozen lump.
detail.watch_for: Bagging them while soft. The pressure of a vacuum seal crushes an unfrozen piece flat.

steps.text: Freeze the uncovered tray for a couple of hours, then transfer to containers.
steps.narration: Slide the open tray into the freezer and come back in a couple of hours to pack them up.

steps.text: Vacuum seal them only if they will sit in the freezer for a while.
steps.narration: Sealing is optional when you plan to eat through them quickly.

detail.how: Freezer burn takes time to develop, so a batch that disappears within days does not need a vacuum sealer. A plain container or zip bag is enough for short-term storage; save the sealing for anything you expect to keep for weeks.
detail.watch_for: Overpacking equipment for a batch you will finish in three days.

steps.text: Reheat from frozen in the microwave for 15 to 30 seconds.
steps.narration: Put a few on a plate and microwave them for 15 to 30 seconds until warm.

detail.how: Time scales with how many are on the plate: a single piece needs only about 15 seconds, a full plate closer to 30 or more. Stop as soon as they are warm through. A glass of milk alongside finishes the job.
detail.watch_for: Blasting a big plateful for one long stretch. The outer pieces go rubbery before the middle ones thaw.

steps.text: Weigh 1 lb (454 g) of frozen broccoli into a microwave-safe dish.
steps.narration: Start with the broccoli: 454 g of it, straight from the freezer bag into a microwave-safe dish.

steps.text: Microwave the broccoli for a minute or two to thaw, then load it into a blender with the yogurt, cheddar and eggs.
steps.narration: Thaw the broccoli in the microwave, then put it in the blender with 600 g of yogurt, 227 g of cheddar and four eggs.

detail.how: One to two minutes is plenty; the broccoli only has to lose its ice, not get hot. Put the broccoli into the jar first so it sits right against the blade, then pile the yogurt, cheese and eggs on top of it.
detail.watch_for: Loading the liquid ingredients first. The broccoli then floats above the blade and you spend the whole time shaking and scraping to get it moving.

steps.text: Lid the jar and blend the mixture.
steps.narration: Put the lid on, set it on the motor and run it.

steps.text: Stop blending once the broccoli looks like a coarse mince rather than a puree.
steps.narration: You want the broccoli broken down to a mince, not liquefied.

detail.how: Watch the texture and cut the motor as soon as the florets read as small even flecks. The mixture should still look grainy, not smooth.
detail.watch_for: Running it too long. Over-blended batter rises less in the oven and the tots come out dense.

steps.text: Weigh 3 1/3 cups (400 g) of oat flour into a large bowl.
steps.narration: Set a big bowl on the scale and add 400 g of oat flour.

detail.how: Oat flour is nothing more than dry oats run through a blender until they are powder, so make your own if you do not have a bag of it. It is far cheaper than buying it milled.
detail.watch_for: Leaving flakes half-broken. Uneven flour hydrates unevenly and the dough stays sticky in patches.

steps.text: Add the onion powder, garlic powder, salt and baking soda, and whisk the dry ingredients together.
steps.narration: Into the flour go 8 g each of onion and garlic powder, 9 g of salt and 8 g of baking soda, then stir.

detail.how: Mixing the dry side thoroughly before any liquid goes in does two jobs: it breaks up the lumps that oat flour always forms, and it spreads the seasoning and the baking soda so no single tot ends up salty or bitter.
detail.watch_for: A pocket of undispersed baking soda, which tastes soapy in whichever tot gets it.

steps.text: Pour the blended mixture into the dry bowl and mix to a dough.
steps.narration: Tip the blender contents into the flour and stir until it comes together.

detail.how: Scrape right around the sides and across the bottom of the bowl as you go. Keep working it until there is no dry flour left anywhere and everything has taken up liquid.
detail.watch_for: Dry patches hiding under the edge of the bowl. They stay powdery through baking.

steps.text: Rest the dough for 5 to 10 minutes, and line your sheet trays with parchment while you wait.
steps.narration: Let the dough sit for 5 to 10 minutes and line the trays in the meantime.

detail.how: Resting lets the oat flour finish absorbing liquid, so the dough thickens and holds a ball shape instead of slumping. This batch filled three sheet trays; with fewer trays, bake in rounds and reuse each one as it empties.
detail.watch_for: Scooping immediately. The dough is still loose and the tots spread into discs.

steps.text: Spray the lined trays with oil and portion the dough with a cookie scoop.
steps.narration: Oil the trays, then start scooping with a number 70 scoop.

detail.how: A number 70 scoop measures about 1 1/4 inches across and holds slightly under a tablespoon. Uniform portions matter here because every tot on the tray has to finish at the same moment.
detail.watch_for: Trying this with a spoon. It works, but shaping well over a hundred equal balls by hand is miserable.

steps.text: Space the balls half an inch to an inch apart and bake at 375F / 190C for about 20 minutes.
steps.narration: Leave half an inch to an inch between them, then bake at 375F / 190C for around 20 minutes.

steps.text: Keep filling trays and send each one into the oven as it is ready, timing them separately.
steps.narration: Carry on scooping while the first tray bakes, and give each tray its own timer.

detail.how: There is no need to have every tray ready at once. Slide each one in as it fills and track its own 20 minutes, since they all went in at different moments. This batch produced 138 tots in total.
detail.watch_for: Running one timer for the whole oven. Later trays come out raw or earlier ones burn.

steps.text: Pull each tray after 20 minutes and set the tots aside to cool.
steps.narration: After 20 minutes take the tray out and start them cooling.

steps.text: Cool completely on the counter, then gather all the tots onto one sheet pan.
steps.narration: Let them cool all the way, then consolidate them onto a single pan for freezing.

detail.how: At my yield of 138 tots each one comes to roughly 24 calories, 2.5 g carbs, 1 g protein and 1.5 g fat. Only pack them once they are fully at room temperature, otherwise residual steam turns to ice in the freezer.
detail.watch_for: Moving them while warm. Trapped heat softens them and they stick to each other.

steps.text: Flash freeze them uncovered in a single layer until solid.
steps.narration: Put the open tray in the freezer and leave it a few hours until they are frozen through.

detail.how: Spreading them out with air around each one lets every tot freeze on its own rather than as a block. Give it a few hours and check that they are hard before doing anything else with them.
detail.watch_for: Bagging them soft. They compress into a solid mass and the texture never recovers.

steps.text: Divide the frozen tots between bags and pull the air out with a vacuum sealer.
steps.narration: Split them across a few bags and vacuum the air out before they go back in the freezer.

detail.how: Three medium bags held this whole batch. Air and moisture next to the food are what cause freezer burn, so drawing the air out is the single most effective thing you can do for long storage. Resealable bags let you take out a portion and pull the air again.
detail.watch_for: One giant bag. Every time you open it the whole batch is exposed.

steps.text: Reheat from frozen in an air fryer at 400F / 204C for 3 to 4 minutes.
steps.narration: For a snack, air fry a handful straight from frozen for 3 or 4 minutes at 400F / 204C.

detail.how: That is long enough to heat the middle through and crisp the outside. Ten or twelve tots makes a sensible portion, which comes to roughly 287 calories and delivers about half a cup of broccoli.
detail.watch_for: Overloading the basket. Piled tots steam each other and stay soft.

steps.text: Reseal the bag and put it straight back in the freezer.
steps.narration: Vacuum the bag again and return it to the freezer while your snack finishes.

title: One Pot Sausage and Pepper Penne

steps.text: Cut the onion into a small dice and the red bell pepper into a large dice.
steps.narration: Dice one medium onion small, then stem, seed and roughly chop one medium red bell pepper.

detail.how: The onion is 200 g and wants a fine dice so it melts into the sauce. The pepper is about 150 g and is deliberately cut bigger, so those red pieces stay visible in the finished pot instead of disappearing.
detail.watch_for: Cutting both the same size, which loses the colour contrast the bigger pepper chunks give you.

steps.text: Smack and mince three cloves of garlic.
steps.narration: Crush three cloves of garlic under the flat of a knife, then chop them fine. That is about 1 tbsp or 15 g.

steps.text: Chop 3 oz (100 g) of baby spinach into small pieces.
steps.narration: Chop the spinach small, or leave the leaves whole if you prefer.

detail.how: Spinach collapses to almost nothing once it hits the hot pot, so chopping is genuinely optional. Cutting it fine simply makes it less noticeable in the finished dish for anyone who is not keen on it.
detail.watch_for: Thinking the raw volume is too much. It shrinks dramatically.

steps.text: Measure out 2 lb (908 g) of 90% lean ground pork.
steps.narration: With the chopping done, weigh out two pounds of lean ground pork.

detail.how: The 90% lean grade keeps the fat in check for the calorie count. If your shop only carries fattier pork, or you do not eat it, ground turkey or ground chicken slots in without changing anything else.
detail.watch_for: A fattier grind, which leaves a slick of grease you will want to spoon off before the pasta goes in.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil in a large pot over medium-high and add the pork.
steps.narration: Get a big pot going over medium-high heat with a spoonful of oil, then add the meat.

detail.how: An 8 quart pot gives you room for everything that follows, including the pasta and the water. Let the oil shimmer before the pork goes in so it starts searing rather than sweating.
detail.watch_for: A pot that is too small. Everything from here on goes into this one vessel.

steps.text: Spread the meat across the base of the pot and let it brown for a couple of minutes.
steps.narration: Press the pork out over the whole surface and leave it alone to colour.

detail.how: Flattening the meat puts as much of it as possible in contact with hot metal, which is where the browning comes from. Resist stirring for the first couple of minutes.
detail.watch_for: Constant stirring. Moved meat gives up water and steams grey instead of browning.

steps.text: Break the meat up once the underside has colour, then add 2 tsp (4 g) of ground fennel.
steps.narration: When the bottom has browned, break the pork apart and start on the sausage seasonings with the fennel.

detail.how: Normally you would season ground meat before cooking so the flavour works its way in, but seasoning it in the pot keeps this to a single dish and saves a step. Fennel is what makes the pork taste like sausage.
detail.watch_for: Breaking it up too early, before any crust has formed on the bottom.

steps.text: Add the smoked paprika, onion powder, garlic powder, salt, oregano and red pepper flakes.
steps.narration: In go 6 g of smoked paprika, 4.5 g each of onion and garlic powder, 9 g of salt, 1 g of oregano and 2 g of red pepper flakes.

steps.text: Add 1 tsp (3 g) of black pepper and stir the seasonings through.
steps.narration: Finish the spice blend with a teaspoon of black pepper and mix it all in.

detail.how: If your shop has no pre-ground fennel, buy whole fennel seed and grind it in a blender, which also avoids biting into whole seeds later.
detail.watch_for: Leaving the red pepper flakes in if heat is not welcome at your table. Drop them entirely and nothing else changes.

steps.text: When the pork is about 90% cooked, clear a well in the middle and add another 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil.
steps.narration: Once the meat is nearly done, push it aside to open a space in the centre and pour in more oil.

steps.text: Put the onion and bell pepper into the well and cook them for 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.narration: Drop the diced onion and pepper into the oiled centre and let them soften.

detail.how: Turn them in the oil so they are coated, but keep them in their own patch rather than folding them into the meat. Giving them direct contact with the pot is what softens them and starts the colour.
detail.watch_for: Mixing them straight into the pork. Buried in meat they only steam and stay raw-tasting.

steps.text: Stir in the garlic, then add 3 tbsp (45 g) of tomato paste and let it caramelize.
steps.narration: Once the onions have taken on colour, add the garlic, mix the whole pot together, then work in the tomato paste.

detail.how: With the garlic in, combine everything so the meat and vegetables are one mixture. Then spread the paste through it and leave it on the heat until it darkens and dries against the pot, which deepens the tomato flavour considerably.
detail.watch_for: Rushing past the paste stage. Raw tomato paste tastes tinny and sharp in the finished sauce.

steps.text: Add one 15 oz (420 g) can of crushed tomatoes, then 10 oz (280 g) of dried penne.
steps.narration: Once the paste has dried out, pour in the crushed tomatoes, stir well, then tip in the penne.

steps.text: Pour in 2 1/2 cups (600 g) of water and make sure the pasta is fully submerged.
steps.narration: Add the water and push the noodles down below the surface.

detail.how: Penne is a sturdier shape than most and holds up over a long cook without going to mush. Any noodle poking above the water line will stay hard, so press everything under before you cover the pot.
detail.watch_for: Pasta stranded above the liquid. Those pieces come out crunchy.

steps.text: Bring to a boil, then cover, drop the heat to low and simmer for 12 to 15 minutes.
steps.narration: Turn the heat up until it boils, then lid it, turn it down low and let it go for 12 to 15 minutes.

detail.how: The boil gets the whole pot up to temperature quickly; the low simmer under a lid then cooks the pasta in the sauce without scorching the bottom. This stretch is hands-off.
detail.watch_for: Leaving the heat high after covering, which sticks the pasta to the base of the pot.

steps.text: Taste a noodle, and once it is cooked through stir in the Parmesan and the spinach.
steps.narration: Fish out a piece of pasta to check it, then add 40 g of grated Parmesan and all the chopped spinach.

detail.how: If the noodle still has bite in the middle, put the lid back on and give it a few more minutes before going further. When it is ready, the cheese and greens go straight into the pot.
detail.watch_for: Adding the spinach before the pasta is done. It overcooks into a dull mush during the extra simmering.

steps.text: Stir until the spinach wilts, then pour in 1/4 cup (60 g) of half and half.
steps.narration: Keep stirring and the mountain of spinach collapses fast, then add the half and half.

detail.how: Half and half keeps the fat lower than cream while still rounding the sauce off. Swap in full heavy cream if you want a richer result and are not counting the calories.
detail.watch_for: Panicking at how much spinach it looks like. It shrinks to a fraction within a minute of stirring.

steps.text: Salt to taste, mix everything together, and divide the pot between five containers.
steps.narration: Adjust the salt, give it a final stir, then split it evenly across five meal prep containers.

steps.text: Split it into more or fewer containers if you want a different calorie count per serving.
steps.narration: Five servings comes to roughly 681 calories and 51 g of protein each, so adjust the count to suit you.

detail.how: Portion size is the only lever here. Take the total nutrition for the whole pot, divide it by however many containers you actually fill, and that is your per-serving figure.
detail.watch_for: Assuming the published numbers hold if you portion differently. They scale with the number of servings.

steps.text: Let the containers cool, put the lids on and refrigerate.
steps.narration: Once cooled, lid them and move them to the fridge, and lunch is sorted for the week.

detail.how: Leave the containers open until they are no longer steaming, otherwise the trapped moisture condenses on the lid and drips back into the pasta. Prep takes roughly 10 minutes for the vegetables and another 10 for the sausage, with the rest largely unattended.
detail.watch_for: Sealing them hot, which waterlogs the pasta by the next day.

ingredients.name: cooking oil, for the carrots and chicken
salt
ingredients.unit: tsp (6 g), plus more to taste

steps.text: Combine the marinade in a large bowl: 1 1/2 tbsp (23 g) each of olive oil, lemon juice and Dijon mustard, 2 tsp (6 g) each of garlic powder and onion powder, 2 tbsp (2 g) dried oregano, 1 tbsp (1 g) dried basil and 1 tsp (6 g) salt.
steps.narration: Measure the oil, lemon juice, mustard, dried herbs and seasonings into a large bowl.

detail.how: Pick a bowl big enough to hold two pounds of chicken afterwards, so you can marinate in the same dish you mixed in. The oil, lemon juice and mustard carry the flavour; the mustard also helps the whole thing hold together instead of separating.
detail.watch_for: Using a bowl that is too small. Once the chicken goes in you need room to toss it without flinging marinade around.

steps.text: Whisk the marinade until it is evenly combined.
steps.narration: Whisk everything together so no dry herbs are left sitting on the surface.

steps.text: Trim 2 lb (908 g) of boneless, skinless chicken thighs and cut them into thin strips.
steps.narration: Cut away loose fat from the thighs, then slice each one into thin fajita-style strips.

detail.how: Thighs are the better choice here because they stay tender even if you push them a little past done. Slice each thigh across into narrow strips roughly the width you would want on a fork, so nothing needs cutting later in the week.
detail.watch_for: Leaving the pieces chunky. Thick pieces take much longer in the skillet and dry out on the outside before the centre is done.

steps.text: Toss the chicken through the marinade and let it sit for about 30 minutes.
