steps.narration: Move the sliced chicken into the marinade and turn it until every piece is coated, then let it rest.

detail.how: Use your hands or tongs and keep folding until you cannot see any bare chicken. Thirty minutes on the counter is plenty for pieces this thin, and the rest of the prep fills that time neatly.
detail.watch_for: Waiting is optional. If you are short on time you can go straight to the skillet, you just get less of the lemon and herb flavour.

steps.text: Peel 2 lb (908 g) of yellow potatoes and chop them into 1 to 2 in pieces.
steps.narration: Peel the potatoes, weigh out two pounds of peeled flesh, and cut them into rough chunks.

detail.how: Weigh the potatoes after peeling, not before, so you actually end up with two pounds in the pot. The pieces get boiled and mashed, so they only need to be roughly the same size as each other, not neatly cut.
detail.watch_for: Wildly uneven chunks. Small pieces fall apart while the big ones are still hard in the middle.

steps.text: Put the potatoes in a large pot with 4 cloves (15 g) of crushed garlic.
steps.narration: Tip the cut potatoes into a big pot and add four crushed cloves of garlic.

detail.how: Lay each clove flat under the side of a knife and press down hard; the skin splits and slips off in one piece. The cloves boil along with the potatoes and go soft enough to mash straight into them.
detail.watch_for: Fishing the garlic out later. It is meant to stay in and get mashed.

steps.text: Cover with water about 2 in above the potatoes, add salt, and boil until a fork slides in easily.
steps.narration: Fill the pot so the water sits a couple of inches over the potatoes, salt it, and bring it up over high heat.

detail.how: Salting the water seasons the potatoes from the inside, which you cannot fully replicate by salting the mash afterwards. Keep it at a steady boil and start testing with a fork after fifteen minutes or so.
detail.watch_for: Pulling them too early. If the fork meets resistance in the centre they will mash lumpy.
detail.duration_hint: Around 15 to 20 minutes at a boil.

steps.text: Wash 1 1/2 lb (681 g) of carrots and cut them on a bias into 1 to 1 1/2 in pieces.
steps.narration: Scrub the carrots well and cut them into large angled pieces.

detail.how: Peeling is optional as long as you scrub them properly. Hold the knife at an angle rather than straight across; the diagonal cut gives each piece a long flat face that sits against the pan and browns.
detail.watch_for: Cutting them small. Little pieces shrink to almost nothing in a hot oven.

steps.text: Toss the carrots with 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil and a heavy pinch or two of salt.
steps.narration: Move the carrots to a bowl, add oil and salt, and turn them until they are evenly slick.

steps.text: Spread the carrots on an oiled sheet pan and bake at 425F / 218C for about 20 minutes.
steps.narration: Lightly oil your biggest sheet pan, spread the carrots across it, and put them in a hot oven.

detail.how: Use the largest pan you own and give the pieces space; anything piled on top of another piece steams instead of roasting. A light spray of oil on the pan keeps them from welding to the metal.
detail.watch_for: Crowding the pan. Two pans beats one overloaded pan every time.

steps.text: Chop about 20 g of parsley for garnish, if you want it.
steps.narration: Optionally chop a small handful of parsley to scatter over the finished bowls.

steps.text: Heat a large skillet over medium-high with a splash of oil and cook the chicken in batches.
steps.narration: Get a large pan hot, add a little oil, and add only as much chicken as fits in one loose layer.

detail.how: Let the pan come up to heat before anything goes in. Add enough chicken to cover the base with gaps still showing between the pieces, and plan on three rounds for two pounds.
detail.watch_for: Tipping the whole bowl in at once. A packed pan traps moisture and the chicken turns grey rather than golden.

steps.text: Leave space between the pieces so the released water can evaporate and the chicken can brown.
steps.narration: Keep gaps in the pan so moisture escapes as steam and the surface colours instead of stewing.

detail.how: Chicken gives up a surprising amount of water as it heats. If there is open pan surface, that water flashes off and the meat can sit against hot metal and take on colour. If there is not, it pools and the chicken poaches in it.
detail.watch_for: Liquid gathering in the pan. That is the signal you have overloaded it.

steps.text: Move each finished batch to a plate and cook the next, splitting 1 tbsp of oil across the batches.
steps.narration: After a couple of minutes, once a batch is cooked through, lift it out and start the next one.

detail.how: Thin strips need only a couple of minutes a side. Share one tablespoon of oil across all the rounds, adding a little at a time as the pan looks dry rather than pouring it all in at the start.
detail.watch_for: Leaving the first batch in while you add the next. It will keep cooking and dry out.
detail.duration_hint: A couple of minutes per batch.

steps.text: At about 12 minutes, toss the carrots and return them to the oven for another 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.narration: Pull the carrot tray partway through and turn the pieces so they colour on all sides.

detail.how: Pull the tray out, shake or turn the carrots so a fresh face lands on the pan, and slide it back in. The pieces touching the metal brown far faster than the ones facing up, so turning them evens things out.
detail.watch_for: Skipping the turn. You end up with one dark side and one pale side on every piece.

steps.text: Set the cooked chicken aside, then drain the tender potatoes and return them to the pot.
steps.narration: Park the last batch of chicken with the rest, then drain the potatoes and tip them back into the dry pot.

detail.how: Test a potato with a fork first; it should slide in with no resistance. Draining them back into the hot pot lets the last of the surface water steam off, which keeps the mash from going watery.
detail.watch_for: Leaving water in the bottom of the pot. It thins the mash and you cannot take it back out.

steps.text: Add 5 tbsp (70 g) of butter and 1/2 cup (120 g) of 2% milk to the potatoes and mash.
steps.narration: Drop the butter and milk into the pot and work the potatoes over with a masher.

detail.how: The butter is doing most of the flavour work, so keep the full amount rather than trimming it. Mash the softened garlic cloves in along with everything else so the flavour spreads through the whole batch.
detail.watch_for: Cutting the butter back. These taste flat without it.

steps.text: Taste the mash and adjust with salt, pepper and extra milk, then mash once more.
steps.narration: Once it is fairly smooth, taste it and correct the seasoning, loosening with more milk if it feels stiff.

detail.how: Add salt in small amounts and taste between each one; it is easy to overshoot and impossible to undo. If the texture is tighter than you like, splash in more milk and give it a final pass with the masher to bring it together.
detail.watch_for: Over-working it. Potatoes beaten too hard turn gluey.

steps.text: Lay out five containers and divide the chicken, carrots and mash evenly between them.
steps.narration: Set out five meal prep containers and split everything five ways.

detail.how: Give the mash its own corner so it does not soak up the carrot oil. Weighing the total and dividing by five gets the portions genuinely even if you care about the calorie numbers.
detail.watch_for: Filling the first two containers generously and running short at the end.

steps.text: Let the containers cool and stop steaming, then lid them and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Wait until the food has stopped giving off steam before you put the lids on, then move them to the fridge.

detail.how: Sealing hot food traps steam that turns to water on the lid and drips back onto the chicken and mash. Leave them open on the counter until they are near room temperature, then cover and refrigerate.
detail.watch_for: Lidding them warm. They keep five days if you let them cool properly first.

steps.text: Reheat in the microwave at 50% power.
steps.narration: When you reheat one, drop the microwave down to half power.

detail.how: Half power heats the food through more gently and evenly, which matters because reheating is effectively a second cook for the chicken. It takes a bit longer but the meat stays tender.
detail.watch_for: Full power. It overcooks the chicken and gives it that rubbery reheated-poultry taste.

ingredients.name: cooking oil, for the chicken and vegetables

steps.text: Cook 3 3/4 cups (562 g) of rice first.
steps.narration: Get the rice going before anything else so it is ready when you plate up.

detail.how: Rice is the one thing here that runs on its own clock, so start it and forget it while the oven work happens. Roughly one cup of dry rice yields about two and a half cups cooked, though it shifts with the grain and the method.
detail.watch_for: Cooking exactly enough. Making a little extra costs nothing and leftover rice is useful all week.

steps.text: Put 2 lb (908 g) of boneless, skinless chicken thighs into a bowl.
steps.narration: Weigh out two pounds of boneless skinless thighs and drop them into a mixing bowl.

steps.text: Add 1 tbsp (15 g) oil, 1 tbsp (15 g) soy sauce and 2 tsp (6 g) garlic powder to the chicken.
steps.narration: Pour the oil and soy sauce over the thighs and add the garlic powder.

steps.text: Add 1/2 tsp (1.5 g) of white pepper if you have it, then toss until the thighs are coated.
steps.narration: White pepper is optional but worth adding, then turn the thighs until they are evenly coated.

detail.how: White pepper brings a slightly earthier heat than black and suits the teriyaki flavours. Turn the pieces over until each one has a thin film of the oil and soy mixture on it; a glove keeps your hands out of the raw chicken.
detail.watch_for: Do not buy white pepper just for this. Skip it if you do not already keep it.

steps.text: Line a sheet pan with foil and set a wire rack on top.
steps.narration: Cover a sheet pan with foil and lay a wire rack over it if you have one.

detail.how: The foil catches everything that drips so the pan barely needs washing. The rack lifts the chicken off the surface, letting hot air circulate underneath instead of the thighs sitting in their own juices.
detail.watch_for: No rack is fine. The chicken just browns a little less on the underside.

steps.text: Spread the chicken in a single layer and bake at 425F / 218C on a bottom rack for 25 minutes.
steps.narration: Lay the thighs out in one layer and put them in a hot oven on a low rack.

detail.how: Keep the pieces apart in one layer so heat reaches all sides. The bottom rack position leaves the upper shelf free for the vegetable tray that goes in shortly after.
detail.watch_for: Overlapping thighs. Where they touch, they steam and stay pale.

steps.text: Cut 1 lb (454 g) of broccoli, about two crowns, into small florets.
steps.narration: Break the broccoli crowns down into florets you can eat in one bite.

detail.how: Aim for pieces that go in your mouth whole but are not so tiny that they collapse in the oven. Cut down through the stem of each floret rather than sawing through the head to keep the buds intact.
detail.watch_for: Cutting them too small. Small florets go mushy and lose their bite.

steps.text: Cut one 300 g sweet potato into pieces about 1/2 in wide and 1 1/2 to 2 in long.
steps.narration: Leave most of the skin on the sweet potato and cut it into long, chunky batons.

detail.how: Trim off only the rough or damaged patches of skin; the rest is fine to eat and saves time. Cutting them larger than usual keeps the interiors soft and sweet rather than drying out, which balances the savoury chicken.
detail.watch_for: Cutting them thin. Thin pieces dry to leather over a long bake.

steps.text: Oil a sheet pan, add the sweet potatoes, sprinkle with salt and toss.
steps.narration: Spray a second pan with oil, tip the sweet potatoes on, season with salt and turn them.

steps.text: Roast the sweet potatoes on a rack above the chicken for about 10 minutes.
steps.narration: Slide the sweet potato pan onto the shelf above the chicken and set a ten minute timer.

detail.how: The sweet potatoes need a head start because they take roughly twice as long as the broccoli. The timer going off is your cue to come back and add the broccoli to the same pan.
detail.watch_for: Adding the broccoli now. It would be burnt long before the potatoes are done.

steps.text: In a small saucepan combine 1/4 cup (60 g) soy sauce, 1/4 cup (60 g) mirin, 1 tbsp (15 g) white vinegar, 3 tbsp (45 g) water, 2 tbsp (24 g) brown sugar and 2 grated cloves (10 g) of garlic, then bring to a light boil.
steps.narration: Measure the teriyaki ingredients into a small saucepan, whisk them together, and bring it up to a gentle boil.

detail.how: Whisk while it heats so the brown sugar dissolves rather than settling on the base and scorching. Grating the garlic instead of chopping it lets it melt into the sauce with no chunks to bite.
detail.watch_for: A hard rolling boil. You want it barely bubbling before you turn it down.

steps.text: Reduce the heat and simmer the sauce for 8 to 10 minutes, whisking now and then.
steps.narration: Turn the heat down and let the sauce simmer, whisking every so often.

detail.how: A low simmer drives off water and concentrates the sauce. Occasional whisking keeps the sugars moving so nothing catches on the bottom of the pan.
detail.watch_for: Walking away entirely. Sugar-heavy sauces burn on the base quickly if left completely alone.

steps.text: When the potato timer sounds, push the potatoes to one side of the pan and add the broccoli.
steps.narration: Pull the vegetable tray, shove the sweet potatoes over, and pour the broccoli into the open space.

detail.how: Give the broccoli a spray of oil and a sprinkle of salt, then toss it around on the pan so the seasoning is spread out. About one tablespoon of oil total covers both the sweet potatoes and the broccoli. Everything goes back in for another 8 to 10 minutes.
detail.watch_for: Dumping the broccoli on top of the potatoes. Keep them side by side so both roast.

steps.text: Check the sauce after about 10 minutes of simmering: it should coat a spoon and bubble around the edges.
steps.narration: Judge the sauce by how it behaves, not by how thick it looks in the pan.

detail.how: Bubbles gathering around the rim of the pot are a good sign it is ready. Lift out a spoonful and pour it back; it should leave a thin film clinging to the metal. It will still look loose while hot, and it firms up considerably as it cools.
detail.watch_for: Reducing it until it looks thick in the pan. Cold, that becomes a solid glaze.

steps.text: Set the sauce aside and take the vegetables and chicken out of the oven.
steps.narration: Park the sauce off the heat, then pull the trays.

detail.how: The sweet potatoes came out at 18 minutes total and the broccoli at 8. The chicken finishes around the same moment, at its full 25 minutes.
detail.watch_for: Leaving the sauce over heat while you deal with the trays. It keeps reducing.

steps.text: Slice the chicken into long strips on a cutting board.
steps.narration: Move the thighs to a board and cut them into strips.

detail.how: Long strips are the classic teriyaki shop cut and they hold sauce well, but any shape works. Cutting now also opens up more surface for the sauce and the broiler to work on.
detail.watch_for: Cutting them too small. Fine pieces dry out fast under the broiler.

steps.text: Return the chicken to the sheet pan, drizzle over 2/3 to 3/4 of the teriyaki sauce, mix, and broil for 5 to 8 minutes.
steps.narration: Put the cut chicken back on the pan, coat it with most of the sauce, and switch the oven to broil.

detail.how: Hold back a quarter to a third of the sauce for drizzling over the finished bowls. Toss the strips so every piece is glazed before the pan goes back in, since the sauce is what browns.
detail.watch_for: Using all the sauce now. You want some left for plating.

steps.text: Stay with the pan while it broils and stir if it colours too fast.
steps.narration: Keep watch under the broiler, especially on a high rack.

detail.how: The nearer the pan sits to the element, the faster it goes from browned to burnt. Leaving the oven door slightly open lets you smell trouble coming, and you can pull the pan and stir things around before anything is lost.
detail.watch_for: Setting a timer and leaving the room. Broilers move much faster than the clock suggests.

steps.text: Taste the chicken once it has good colour and adjust with salt.
steps.narration: When the browning looks right, taste a piece and add salt if it needs it.

steps.text: Lay out five containers, add 3/4 cup (112 g) of rice to each, and divide the rest evenly.
steps.narration: Set out five meal prep containers, portion the rice, then split the chicken and vegetables five ways.

detail.how: Put the rice down first so it forms a base for everything else. Weighing each rice portion keeps the servings honest if you are tracking the numbers.
detail.watch_for: Eyeballing the first containers generously and coming up short on the last.

steps.text: Drizzle the reserved teriyaki sauce over the chicken and add sesame seeds if you like.
steps.narration: Spoon the sauce you held back over the chicken in each container and finish with sesame seeds.

detail.how: The sauce thickens noticeably once it cools in the containers, so it will not run everywhere. Sesame seeds are purely for looks and add nothing you would miss.
detail.watch_for: Pouring it over the rice instead. Keep it on the chicken so the rice does not go soggy.

steps.text: Let the containers cool, put the lids on and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Once they have cooled down, cover them and move them into the fridge.

detail.how: Lidding food while it is still hot traps steam that condenses and drips back down, which turns the rice and broccoli watery. Leave them open until they are close to room temperature first.
detail.watch_for: Sealing them warm. Given a proper cool-down they hold for five days.

ingredients.name: salt
ingredients.unit: tsp (6 g), plus more for the chicken

steps.text: Gather 1/2 lb (227 g) each of frozen cauliflower and frozen butternut squash.
steps.narration: Start with frozen vegetables so there is nothing to wash or chop.

detail.how: Frozen produce comes already trimmed and cut, which removes the messiest part of the prep. If your shop has no frozen butternut squash, a full pound of frozen cauliflower works, and frozen carrots substitute fine too.
detail.watch_for: Reaching for fresh vegetables. The whole point of this one is that nothing needs a knife.

steps.text: Microwave the frozen vegetables for a few minutes to thaw and warm them.
steps.narration: Put the frozen vegetables in the microwave to warm through while you deal with the chicken.

steps.text: Cut 1 1/2 lb (681 g) of boneless, skinless chicken thighs into bite-sized pieces directly in a 16 by 9 in casserole dish.
steps.narration: Cut the chicken straight into the baking dish rather than onto a board.

detail.how: Working over the dish itself means no cutting board picks up raw chicken, which is one less thing to scrub afterwards. Thighs stay juicier through the long bake; breast works but comes out noticeably drier.
detail.watch_for: Using a board out of habit. The whole shortcut is that the dish catches everything.

steps.text: Use kitchen shears to cut the thighs up and trim away any thick fat as you go.
steps.narration: Shears are faster than a knife here and let you trim fat in the same motion.

detail.how: Hold a thigh over the dish and snip it into small pieces, working around any heavy pads of fat and dropping those aside. Small pieces matter because they need to cook through in the same time as the pasta.
detail.watch_for: Leaving chunks too big. They stay underdone in the middle of the bake.

steps.text: Spread the chicken across the bottom of the dish and sprinkle salt over it.
steps.narration: Level the chicken out over the base of the dish and season it with salt.

detail.how: An even layer matters structurally as well as for cooking, because the chicken becomes the platform the pasta rests on. Add any other seasonings you like at this point.
detail.watch_for: Piling it in one corner. Bare patches of dish let the pasta sit flat against the base.

steps.text: Into a blender add 1 cup (227 g) cottage cheese, 1 1/2 cups (360 g) 2% milk, 1 1/2 cups (360 g) water, 2 tsp (10 g) chicken bouillon, 1 tsp (6 g) salt and 1 tsp (3 g) onion powder.
steps.narration: Set the blender jug on a scale and add the cottage cheese, milk, water, bouillon, salt and onion powder.

detail.how: Weighing straight into the jug on a scale saves washing measuring cups. Cottage cheese is what makes this creamy without cream, and the bouillon supplies the savoury backbone in place of a stock.
detail.watch_for: Forgetting to zero the scale between additions.

steps.text: Add 1 tsp (3 g) each of garlic powder and black pepper, 1 tbsp (1 g) dried Italian seasoning, 2 tsp (10 g) lemon juice, 1 1/2 tbsp (22.5 g) oil and all the warmed vegetables.
steps.narration: Add the remaining seasonings, the lemon juice, the oil and the thawed vegetables to the blender.

steps.text: Blend until the vegetables are completely smooth and nothing is recognisable.
steps.narration: Run the blender until the sauce is uniform with no vegetable pieces left.

detail.how: Keep it going past the point where it looks done; any flecks of cauliflower left whole will show up in the finished dish. Blended right in, the vegetables add bulk and nutrition without anyone having to notice them.
detail.watch_for: Stopping too soon. Half-blended cauliflower gives a gritty, grainy sauce.

steps.text: Weigh out 10 oz (280 g) of dry spaghetti.
steps.narration: Measure the spaghetti and keep it to hand, dry and uncooked.

steps.text: Pour a layer of sauce over the chicken, then lay some of the spaghetti on top.
steps.narration: Cover the chicken with sauce first, then set down a layer of dry spaghetti.

detail.how: The chicken pieces hold the pasta slightly off the base of the dish, so liquid can get all the way around each strand. That gap is what lets the spaghetti cook evenly with no boiling step.
detail.watch_for: Dry spaghetti pressed flat against the bottom of the dish. It never softens and you get hard pockets.

steps.text: Keep alternating sauce and spaghetti until both are used up, coating every strand.
steps.narration: Build up the layers until the dish holds all of the pasta and all of the sauce.

detail.how: After each layer of pasta, ladle enough sauce over to submerge it before adding more. Run your eye over the top before it goes in the oven; any strand sitting dry will stay dry.
detail.watch_for: Dumping all the pasta in at once. Layering is what guarantees full coverage.

steps.text: Cover the dish tightly with foil and bake at 375F / 190C for 45 minutes.
steps.narration: Seal the dish under foil and put it in the oven for three quarters of an hour.

detail.how: A tight seal keeps the steam inside, which is what cooks the pasta and the chicken through. Press the foil down around the rim rather than just draping it over the top.
detail.watch_for: A loose cover. Escaping steam leaves the top layer of pasta undercooked.

steps.text: Take the foil off and stir the bake.
steps.narration: Pull the foil away and give everything a stir straight out of the oven.

detail.how: The sauce will look far too thin at this moment, which is normal. Stirring drags the starch the spaghetti has shed through the whole dish, and that starch is what thickens it as it cools.
detail.watch_for: Panicking at the thin sauce and adding thickener. Give it time instead.

steps.text: Stir gently to avoid breaking the noodles and separate any clumps into single strands.
steps.narration: Work carefully through the dish, teasing stuck-together noodles apart.

detail.how: Move the spoon slowly and lift rather than scrape, so the softened spaghetti stays long. Where strands have fused into a clump, pull them apart so sauce can reach the surfaces in between.
detail.watch_for: Stirring hard. Baked spaghetti snaps easily and you end up with short stubs.

steps.text: Rest the dish on the counter for 15 to 20 minutes until the sauce thickens, then lay out five containers and divide it evenly.
steps.narration: Leave it to cool and firm up, then split it between five meal prep containers.

detail.how: The change over those fifteen to twenty minutes is dramatic; what looked soupy sets into a proper creamy sauce. Only portion once it has thickened, otherwise the liquid pools unevenly across the containers.
detail.watch_for: Plating it straight from the oven. You will end up with soup in some tubs and pasta in others.

steps.text: Spread 1/2 cup (56 g) of shaved Parmesan cheese over the five dishes.
steps.narration: Weigh out the Parmesan and share it across the tops of all five containers.

steps.text: Top each container with a little fresh chopped parsley.
steps.narration: Scatter chopped parsley over each one for a bit of colour.

steps.text: Put the lids on and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Cover the containers and move them into the fridge for the week.

steps.text: Reheat in the microwave for a few minutes at 50 to 60% power until hot.
steps.narration: Warm a portion through at just over half power rather than full blast.

detail.how: Lower power heats the pasta and chicken through evenly instead of scorching the edges. If the sauce has set firmer than you want after a few days in the fridge, stir in a splash of milk before it goes in.
detail.watch_for: Full power. It dries the chicken and can split the sauce.

ingredients.name: top round beef (London broil) or top sirloin
salt
ingredients.unit: tsp (6 g), plus more to taste

ingredients.name: black pepper
ingredients.unit: tsp (3 g), plus more to taste

steps.text: Peel one medium onion (200 g) and cut it into a small dice.
steps.narration: Start with the vegetables. Strip the papery skin off the onion and chop it small.

steps.text: Cut 1 lb (454 g) of carrots into strips, then across into 1 in pieces.
steps.narration: Cut the carrots into batons and then into inch-long chunks.

detail.how: Peeling is optional here. Shave off anything on the outside that looks unappealing and move on. Keep the pieces chunky, roughly an inch each, because they sit in hot liquid and small pieces disappear.
detail.watch_for: Cutting them thin or fine. In a slow cooker that turns them to mush with no bite left.

steps.text: Cut 8 oz (227 g) of mushrooms into quarters, or into sixths or eighths if they are large.
steps.narration: Quarter the mushrooms, cutting the bigger ones into more pieces so they end up a similar size.

detail.how: Aim for pieces roughly the size of the carrot chunks so nothing looks out of place in the finished dish. If mushrooms are not for you, leave them out entirely; nothing else in the recipe depends on them.
detail.watch_for: Wildly uneven pieces, which cook at different rates in the last half hour.

steps.text: Choose your beef: top round, also sold as London broil, or top sirloin.
steps.narration: Pick a lean cut. Top round is cheap and very lean, and the long cook softens it.

detail.how: Top round has almost no marbling running through it, which is why it is inexpensive and why it starts out tough. Hours in the slow cooker break it down. Top sirloin is similarly lean, comes out more tender, and costs more, so pick whichever suits your budget.
detail.watch_for: Buying a fatty cut instead. The extra fat renders into the sauce and makes it greasy once chilled.

steps.text: Add 2 1/2 cups (600 g) beef broth, 1 tbsp (15 g) Worcestershire sauce, 1 tsp (6 g) salt and 2 tsp (6 g) garlic powder to the slow cooker.
steps.narration: Build the cooking liquid straight in the slow cooker pot with broth, Worcestershire and the first seasonings.

steps.text: Add 2 tsp (6 g) paprika and 1 tsp (3 g) pepper, stir the diced onion through, then lay 2 1/2 lb (1.35 kg) of beef on top.
steps.narration: Finish the seasoning, stir in the onion, and settle the beef into the liquid.

detail.how: Stir until the powdered spices have dispersed rather than sitting in clumps on the surface, then set the whole piece of beef down into the broth. The onion goes in at the start on purpose; it has all day to fall apart and sweeten the sauce.
detail.watch_for: Dropping the beef in before mixing, which traps dry spice underneath it.

steps.text: Cover and cook on high for about 4 hours, or on low for 6.
steps.narration: Put the lid on and let the slow cooker do the work.

detail.how: Searing the beef in a skillet beforehand would add a little roasted flavour, but it is genuinely optional and the dish is good without that extra pan. Set it and leave it alone; lifting the lid to peek costs you heat every time.
detail.watch_for: Opening the lid repeatedly, which stretches the cook time out.
detail.duration_hint: 4 hours on high or 6 on low.

steps.text: With 30 minutes of cook time left, add the carrots and mushrooms and stir them under the liquid.
steps.narration: Near the end, tip the carrots and mushrooms in and push them below the surface.

detail.how: Half an hour is enough for the carrots to turn tender while keeping a bit of bite. Stir until they are submerged so they cook in liquid rather than sitting dry above it, then put the lid back on for the final stretch.
detail.watch_for: Adding them at the start. Four hours reduces them to mush with no texture left.

steps.text: Bring a large pot of water to a boil over high heat.
steps.narration: While the vegetables finish, get a big pot of water boiling.

steps.text: Cook 24 oz (681 g) of pasta in the boiling water.
steps.narration: Drop the pasta into the boiling water and cook it through.

detail.how: That is a lot of pasta, and it is deliberate: the noodles carry most of the calories in these portions. Any shape works, and gluten-free pasta is a straight swap if you need it. Use the biggest pot you own so the water is not overwhelmed.
detail.watch_for: Cooking it very soft. It keeps softening in the sauce over the following days.

steps.text: Stir 3 tbsp (24 g) cornstarch into 1/4 cup (60 g) cold water to make a slurry, then drain the pasta.
steps.narration: Mix the cornstarch with cold water in a small bowl, then drain the cooked noodles and set them aside.

detail.how: The water has to be cold. Cornstarch dropped into anything warm seizes into lumps immediately, whereas in cold water it stays suspended and pours smoothly. Stir it again right before you use it, because it settles to the bottom within a minute.
detail.watch_for: Letting the slurry stand and pouring off the thin water at the top.

steps.text: Lift the cooked beef into a large bowl, then drizzle the slurry into the hot liquid and stir.
steps.narration: Take the beef out, then thicken the sauce left behind with the cornstarch slurry.

detail.how: The liquid needs to still be hot for the starch to activate, so do this straight after the beef comes out. Pour in a thin stream while stirring rather than dumping it all at once.
detail.watch_for: Adding the whole slurry blindly. How much you need depends on how much water the beef gave up.

steps.text: Keep adding slurry until the sauce coats the back of a spoon.
steps.narration: Judge the thickness by dipping a spoon: the sauce should cling to it.

detail.how: Dip a spoon in and lift it out. If a film stays on the metal rather than running straight off, you are done. Stop a shade thinner than you want, because the noodles keep absorbing liquid and the sauce firms up considerably over a few days in the fridge.
detail.watch_for: Thickening it to a paste on day one. By day three it will be stodgy.

steps.text: Break the beef into bite-sized chunks, return it to the sauce and stir to coat.
steps.narration: Pull the beef apart into bite-sized pieces and stir them back into the thickened sauce.

detail.how: A fork in one hand and a butter knife in the other is enough; the meat should give way with almost no pressure. Two forks pulled in opposite directions will shred it finer if you prefer smaller strands. Once it is all broken down, tip it back into the pot and fold until every piece is coated.
detail.watch_for: Beef that resists being pulled apart. That means it needs more time in the cooker.

steps.text: Stir in 2/3 cup (150 g) plain 2% Greek yogurt and 2/3 cup (150 g) cream cheese.
steps.narration: Add the yogurt and cream cheese for creaminess.

detail.how: Splitting the dairy between yogurt and cream cheese gives you the tang and richness of a classic stroganoff without the fat of full cream. Cutting the cream cheese into smaller pieces first helps it melt into the sauce faster.
detail.watch_for: Rushing it. Cold cream cheese needs a minute in the warm sauce before it will blend smoothly.

steps.text: Add 1 tbsp (15 g) Dijon mustard, mix until smooth, then taste and adjust with salt and pepper.
steps.narration: Stir the Dijon through, mix until the cream cheese has fully melted, then taste and season.

detail.how: Keep mixing until you cannot see any pale streaks of cream cheese. Then taste it properly on a spoon and correct the salt and pepper now, while the sauce is on its own and easy to judge.
detail.watch_for: Seasoning after the pasta goes in. The noodles dull everything and you will need far more salt to fix it.

steps.text: Tip in all the cooked noodles and stir until they are coated.
steps.narration: Add the drained pasta and fold everything together until the sauce covers it all.

steps.text: If your slow cooker is too small to hold it all, put plain noodles in the containers and ladle the sauce over instead.
steps.narration: With a smaller pot, split the job: noodles in the containers first, sauce spooned over the top.

detail.how: This is a big volume of food. An eight quart cooker holds it comfortably; anything smaller and you will be pushing pasta over the rim trying to stir. Portioning the noodles out first and topping each one with sauce gets you the same meal without the mess.
detail.watch_for: Forcing it into a full pot and losing half of it over the side.

steps.text: Lay out five meal prep containers and weigh one empty.
steps.narration: Set out five containers and note what an empty one weighs.

detail.how: Knowing the empty weight lets you subtract it later, so the scale tells you how much food is actually in each container rather than food plus plastic. Note the number down or leave the scale zeroed on an empty one.
detail.watch_for: Skipping this and then wondering why the numbers do not line up.

steps.text: Divide everything between the five containers, weighing each and shuffling food until they match.
steps.narration: Share the stroganoff out evenly, then check each on the scale and move food around to level them.

detail.how: Fill all five roughly by eye first, then weigh them one at a time and move a spoonful from the heaviest to the lightest until they land close together. If you want, finish each with a scattering of chopped parsley, which is purely for looks.
detail.watch_for: Filling the first containers generously and running short on the last one.

steps.text: Let the meals stop steaming, lid them and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Wait until the steam has died down, then put the lids on and move them to the fridge.

detail.how: Sealing hot food traps steam that condenses and thins the sauce, so leave the containers open until they stop giving off visible heat. If the portions are more food than you need, halving every quantity in the recipe gives you the same dish at half the calories and protein.
detail.watch_for: Lidding them while hot. Expect watery sauce and soggy pasta by the next day.

ingredients.name: chickpea pasta, or any short shape
salt, divided
ingredients.unit: 3 g in the marinade, 2 g in the dressing, plus more at the table

steps.text: In a bowl on a scale, combine 2 tsp (10 g) oil, 1 1/3 tbsp (20 g) lemon juice, 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt, 1/2 tsp (2 g) each of onion powder, garlic powder and cumin, and 1 tsp (1 g) dried oregano.
steps.narration: Start the chicken, since it takes longest. Build the marinade in a large bowl set on a scale.

detail.how: Setting the bowl on a scale and zeroing between additions means you never wash a measuring spoon. Use a bowl big enough to hold the chicken afterwards so you are not moving things around later.
detail.watch_for: Forgetting to re-zero the scale between ingredients, which throws off everything after it.

steps.text: Add 1/4 tsp (1 g) cayenne, stir the marinade smooth, then add 1 1/2 lb (681 g) chicken breasts and toss to coat.
steps.narration: Finish the marinade with cayenne, mix it, then turn the chicken breasts through it.

steps.text: Lay the chicken in a casserole dish, cover with foil and bake at 400F / 204C for about 25 minutes, until it holds 155F for at least a minute.
steps.narration: Transfer the chicken to a baking dish, cover it tightly with foil and bake it.

detail.how: The foil traps steam and keeps the breasts from drying out, which matters because chicken breast has almost no fat to protect it. Judge doneness with a thermometer rather than the clock: it needs to sit at 155F for a full minute, not just touch it.
detail.watch_for: Overcooking. Chicken breast is unforgiving, and this batch never gets reheated to hide it.

steps.text: Pick your pasta shape.
steps.narration: Choose whatever pasta you like. Chickpea pasta adds fibre if that is something you are chasing.

detail.how: Chickpea pasta brings noticeably more fibre than wheat pasta, at the cost of a slightly firmer, grainier bite. Any regular short shape works just as well if you would rather have the softer texture.
detail.watch_for: Long strands. Short shapes are far easier to eat cold out of a container.

steps.text: Cook the pasta in boiling water.
steps.narration: Get the pasta into boiling water and cook it through.

steps.text: In a second bowl, combine 6 tbsp (90 g) olive oil, 1/4 cup (60 g) red wine vinegar and 1 tbsp (15 g) lemon juice, then grate in 2 cloves (10 g) of garlic.
steps.narration: Build the dressing. Grate the garlic rather than chopping it.

detail.how: Grating the garlic on a fine rasp breaks the cloves down into a paste that dissolves into the dressing, so the flavour spreads through every bite instead of hiding in occasional chunks.
detail.watch_for: Rough chopping the garlic. You get harsh raw bites in some forkfuls and nothing in others.

steps.text: Add 2 tsp (2 g) dried oregano, 1/3 tsp (2 g) salt and 1/2 tsp (2 g) pepper, then whisk to emulsify.
steps.narration: Season the dressing and whisk it hard until the oil and vinegar come together.

detail.how: Whisk briskly until the mixture goes from two separate layers to one cloudy liquid. It will separate again while it sits, which is normal, so plan to give it another whisk before it goes on the salad.
detail.watch_for: A lazy stir. Unemulsified dressing pours out as oil first and vinegar last.

steps.text: Peel some skin off one cucumber, scrape out the seeds with a spoon, then cut it into a medium dice to yield 150 g.
steps.narration: Part-peel the cucumber, scoop the seedy middle out, and dice the rest.

detail.how: Taking off some of the peel softens the bite without losing all the colour. Halve the cucumber lengthways and run a teaspoon down the middle to lift out the watery seed core, then cut the firm flesh into even pieces. English cucumbers work nicely but any type will do.
detail.watch_for: Leaving the seeds in. They release water and leave a puddle in the bottom of your containers.

steps.text: Cut 8 oz (227 g) of grape tomatoes into halves or quarters.
steps.narration: Halve or quarter the grape tomatoes.

detail.how: The trick of trapping tomatoes between two container lids and slicing through the gap is popular online but tends to squash more than it cuts. Halving them one by one on a board with a sharp serrated knife is slower but far less messy.
detail.watch_for: A blunt knife, which crushes the tomatoes and drains their juice onto the board.

steps.text: Slice one small red onion (125 g) thinly, then rinse and soak the slices in cold water.
steps.narration: Cut the red onion into thin slices, then leave them sitting in cold water while you do everything else.

detail.how: The cold soak washes away the sulphur compounds that make raw onion sharp, leaving it milder and more pleasant to eat uncooked. Let them sit while you finish the rest of the prep, then drain them well before they go in the bowl.
detail.watch_for: Skipping the soak. Raw red onion overpowers everything else in a cold salad.
detail.duration_hint: As long as the rest of the prep takes.

steps.text: Pull the chicken from the oven, check the thickest breast with a thermometer, and set it aside to cool.
steps.narration: When the timer goes, take the chicken out and probe the biggest piece to confirm it is up to temperature.

detail.how: Push the probe into the middle of the largest breast, since that is the last part to come up to temperature. If it reads short, cover it back up and give it a few more minutes rather than guessing.
detail.watch_for: Testing a small piece. It will read done while the big one is still under.

steps.text: Drain the pasta, rinse it under cool water to stop the cooking, and tip it into a large bowl.
steps.narration: Drain the noodles and run cold water over them, then move them to a big mixing bowl.

detail.how: Rinsing does two things here: it drops the temperature so the pasta stops cooking in its own heat, and it washes off surface starch that would otherwise glue the salad together. Shake the colander well so you are not adding water to the dressing.
detail.watch_for: Leaving hot pasta to sit. It keeps softening and will wilt the spinach later.

steps.text: Add the drained red onion, the tomatoes, the cucumber and 5 oz (150 g) of baby spinach to the bowl.
steps.narration: Pile the vegetables in with the pasta: onion, tomatoes, cucumber and a big handful of baby spinach.

steps.text: Whisk the dressing once more, pour it over and toss until every piece is coated.
steps.narration: Re-whisk the dressing, tip it in and toss thoroughly.

detail.how: Keep turning the bowl over from the bottom until the spinach leaves, the noodles and the cut faces of the vegetables all carry dressing. Do this before the chicken goes in: chicken soaks up dressing greedily, and you want it on the vegetables instead.
detail.watch_for: Under-mixing. Dressing settles at the bottom and the top layer tastes of nothing.

steps.text: Chill the cooked chicken in the freezer, then slice it thin.
steps.narration: Firm the chicken up in the freezer, then cut it into thin slices.

detail.how: A short spell in the freezer firms the meat so the knife glides instead of tearing. Slice it as thinly as you can manage. Eaten cold, thin slices stay tender, while thick chunks turn rubbery and dry in the mouth.
detail.watch_for: Cutting it warm into big cubes. That is the version people complain about.
detail.duration_hint: Long enough to firm up, not to freeze.

steps.text: Add the sliced chicken and 1 cup (112 g) of crumbled feta, and mix everything together.
steps.narration: Scoop the chicken into the bowl, scatter the feta over and fold it all through.

steps.text: Divide the salad evenly between five meal prep containers of at least 28 oz.
steps.narration: Set out five containers and share the salad between them.

detail.how: Raw spinach and vegetables take up a lot of room, so this fills bigger containers than a cooked meal of the same weight would. Around 28 oz per container gives you space to mix it later without spilling.
detail.watch_for: Small containers. You will not be able to stir in the salt before eating.

steps.text: Lid the containers and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Put the lids on and move them into the fridge for the week.

detail.how: Nothing here is hot, so the lids can go straight on and the containers go into the fridge immediately. A drained can of cannellini beans stirred through at this point adds a little more protein and fibre if you want it.
detail.watch_for: Nothing tricky. This one is designed to be eaten straight from the fridge with no reheating.

steps.text: Leave the salad lightly salted while it is stored.
steps.narration: Resist the urge to salt the vegetables heavily now. It is deliberately under-seasoned in storage.

detail.how: Salt draws water out of tomatoes and cucumber. Over several days in a sealed container that liquid collects at the bottom and turns the whole thing soupy, so the seasoning is held back on purpose.
detail.watch_for: Salting to taste on prep day and finding a pool of liquid on day three.

steps.text: Sprinkle salt over the portion just before eating and mix it in.
steps.narration: When you are ready to eat, add a pinch of salt, stir it through and dig in.

ingredients.name: canned black beans, drained and rinsed
salt
ingredients.unit: tsp (3 g), plus more to taste

steps.text: Cut 1 1/2 lb (681 g) of top sirloin into thin strips about 2 in long and 1/4 in wide.
steps.narration: Start with the steak. Slice it into thin fajita-style strips.

detail.how: Use the sharpest knife you own; a dull blade drags and tears rather than slicing cleanly. Aim for strips roughly two inches long and a quarter inch wide, the same size you would cut for fajitas. Thin and even matters more than exact measurements.
detail.watch_for: Thick strips. They take longer in the pan and turn chewy once reheated.

steps.text: Trim away any excess fat, then in a large bowl on a scale combine 1 tbsp (15 g) each of soy sauce, lime juice and oil.
steps.narration: Cut off the fatty bits as you go, then start the marinade in a big bowl.

steps.text: Stir in 1 tbsp (12 g) chili powder, 1 tsp (3 g) each of onion powder, garlic powder and black pepper, 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and 1/4 tsp (2 g) baking soda.
steps.narration: Add the dry seasonings and the baking soda, and mix until evenly combined.

detail.how: Mix the liquids and powders into a smooth paste before the meat goes anywhere near it, otherwise the spices clump on a few pieces and leave the rest bare. The baking soda is measured small on purpose; more than a quarter teaspoon starts to taste soapy.
detail.watch_for: Eyeballing the baking soda. Too much leaves a metallic aftertaste.

steps.text: Tip all the sliced beef into the marinade.
steps.narration: Add the steak strips to the bowl.

detail.how: The baking soda here is doing real work: it raises the surface pH of the meat so the proteins hold onto moisture instead of squeezing it out. That is what keeps the steak from going tough when it is reheated in a microwave later in the week.
detail.watch_for: Skipping the baking soda if you plan to reheat. This is the step that saves the texture.

steps.text: Mix the beef by hand, squeezing the pieces until every one is coated, then set it aside.
steps.narration: Get your hands in and work the marinade through the meat, squeezing as you go.

detail.how: Hands do a better job than a spoon here because you can feel which pieces are still dry. Squeezing and pressing the strips also physically loosens the muscle fibres, which helps tenderise alongside the baking soda. Be firm with it.
detail.watch_for: Gentle stirring. Half the strips end up with no marinade on them.

steps.text: Rinse 1 1/2 cups (270 g) of dry long grain rice until the water runs clear, then cook it with about 2 1/4 cups (340 g) of water.
steps.narration: Wash the rice until the runoff is no longer cloudy, then get it cooking.

detail.how: Rinsing washes off loose surface starch so the grains stay separate rather than gluing together. In a rice cooker, fill with water to just under the 2 cup line. On the stovetop use around 2 1/4 cups of water for this amount of rice.
detail.watch_for: Cooking it unrinsed, which gives you a sticky mass that is awkward to portion.

steps.text: Cut one medium red bell pepper (150 g) into a small dice.
steps.narration: While the rice cooks and the steak marinates, chop the vegetables, starting with the bell pepper.

steps.text: Roughly chop one small jalapeno (20 to 30 g) and 2 stalks (20 g) of green onions.
steps.narration: Chop the jalapeno and green onions roughly. Neatness does not matter here.

detail.how: These are heading into a blender, so any size will do. If you want the rice mild, scrape out the jalapeno seeds and the pale ribs inside first, since that is where nearly all of the heat sits.
detail.watch_for: Spending time on a fine chop that the blender will undo anyway.

steps.text: Blend the jalapeno, green onions, 1/2 cup (30 g) of chopped cilantro and 1/4 cup (60 g) of water until smooth.
steps.narration: Put the herbs and chilli in a blender with water and run it until it turns green and loose.

detail.how: Cilantro stems go in along with the leaves; they carry plenty of flavour and disappear in the blender. The water is there to give the blades something to move, so do not leave it out or the mixture just packs against the sides.
detail.watch_for: Blending it dry. Without the water it will not circulate and you get a paste stuck to the walls.

steps.text: Check the blend for large chunks of onion or jalapeno, then set it aside.
steps.narration: It does not need to be perfectly smooth, just free of big pieces.

detail.how: A few flecks of cilantro leaf still visible in the mixture are fine and even look good stirred through rice. What you are checking for is chunks of raw onion or chilli, which would be unpleasant to bite into.
detail.watch_for: Over-blending to a puree. There is no benefit and you lose the flecks.

steps.text: Heat a large skillet over medium-high, about 7.5 out of 10, with 1/2 tbsp (7.5 g) of oil.
steps.narration: Get a big skillet properly hot with a little oil in it.

detail.how: The steak will be cooked in two batches so the pan never gets crowded, which is the difference between browned meat and grey steamed meat. Half the oil goes in now and half with the second batch, one tablespoon in total.
detail.watch_for: A pan that is not hot enough yet. The steak will release water instead of searing.

steps.text: Spread half the steak across the pan with space between the pieces and leave it for 1 to 2 minutes, then flip.
steps.narration: Lay the first batch out in one layer, leave it alone to colour, then turn it over.

detail.how: Give the strips room, and then genuinely leave them alone. Colour only develops where meat sits still against hot metal, so poking and stirring in the first minute or two undoes the whole point of the batch cooking.
detail.watch_for: Stirring straight away. That is the most common reason home-cooked steak strips come out pale.
detail.duration_hint: 1 to 2 minutes before the first flip.

steps.text: Take the first batch out, return the pan to the heat with the remaining 1/2 tbsp (7.5 g) of oil, and cook the rest of the beef for about 2 minutes a side.
steps.narration: Move the seared steak to a plate, oil the pan again and repeat with the second batch.

detail.how: Cut this thin, the strips cook through quickly. Roughly two minutes on each side is enough to get good colour on both faces without drying the middle out.
detail.watch_for: Leaving it in longer for safety. Thin strips overcook in seconds.

steps.text: Weigh out 1 cup (170 g) of frozen corn kernels.
steps.narration: While the second batch cooks, measure out the frozen corn.

steps.text: Drain and rinse one 15.5 oz (430 g) can of black beans, then add the first batch of steak back to the pan.
steps.narration: Rinse the beans in a sieve, then return the reserved steak to the skillet with the rest.

detail.how: Rinsing the beans washes off the thick, salty canning liquid, which otherwise makes everything it touches taste of the can. Bringing both batches back together now means the glaze coats all the meat at once.
detail.watch_for: Tipping the can in undrained. That liquid muddies the honey lime flavour.

steps.text: Stir in 1 tbsp (21 g) honey and 1 tbsp (15 g) lime juice, cook 1 to 2 minutes more so the honey can caramelize, then salt to taste and move the steak to a plate.
steps.narration: Drizzle over the honey and lime, toss the steak in it, and let it cook another minute or two.

detail.how: As the honey hits the hot pan it reduces and caramelises around the outside of each strip, which is where the flavour of this dish comes from. Keep the meat moving so the sugar coats rather than settling and scorching. Taste and add salt before it leaves the pan.
detail.watch_for: Leaving it too long. Honey goes from caramelised to burnt and bitter fast.

steps.text: Put the same skillet back over medium-high heat with 1 tbsp (15 g) of oil, then add the 1 cup (170 g) of frozen corn and the diced bell pepper.
steps.narration: Reuse the skillet for the vegetables. Add oil, then the corn and pepper.

detail.how: Cooking the vegetables in the pan the steak came out of saves washing up and picks up the browned bits and leftover glaze stuck to the surface, which is free flavour.
detail.watch_for: Reaching for a second clean pan out of habit.

steps.text: Cook only until the peppers soften and the corn thaws, then season with salt.
steps.narration: This is quick. Once the pepper has softened and the corn is hot through, season and stop.

detail.how: You are barely cooking these, just taking the raw edge off the pepper and warming the corn through. Any green onion left over from the rice blend can be chopped and thrown in at this point too.
detail.watch_for: Cooking them down until soft. The bowls want some crunch left in the pepper.

steps.text: Pour the green blend into the cooked rice, stir it through, then replace the lid and steam for another 5 to 7 minutes.
steps.narration: When the rice is done, mix the herb blend in, cover it again and let it sit and steam.

detail.how: Fold the green mixture through until the colour is even all the way to the bottom of the pot, then close the lid. The residual heat drives off the extra liquid you added with the blend and lets the flavour settle into the grains. Cooking on the stovetop, do this once the simmer is off.
detail.watch_for: Serving it straight after mixing. It tastes raw and watery without the steam rest.

steps.text: Measure 2 tbsp (30 g) of salsa into each of five ramekins.
steps.narration: While the rice rests, portion the salsa into small ramekins.

steps.text: Taste the rested rice and adjust it with salt, then lay out five meal prep containers.
steps.narration: Try the rice, correct the salt, and get five containers ready.

steps.text: Divide the rice, steak, vegetables and the drained beans evenly between the five containers.
steps.narration: Share everything out across the five containers.

detail.how: Five identical containers make it easy to portion by eye: fill them side by side and compare as you go. The beans need no cooking at all; they go in straight from the sieve and warm up when the meal is microwaved.
detail.watch_for: Nothing serious. Small differences between containers even out over a week of eating them.

steps.text: Clear a small well in one corner of each container and set a ramekin of salsa into it.
steps.narration: Push the food aside in one corner and nestle a salsa ramekin into the gap.

steps.text: Let the bowls cool and stop steaming, then lid them and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Once they have cooled down, put the lids on and move them to the fridge.

detail.how: Sealing warm containers traps steam that condenses on the lid and drips back onto the rice, making it wet. Wait until you can no longer see steam rising before closing them.
detail.watch_for: Lidding them hot, which leaves soggy rice by the second day.

steps.text: For a faster version, use ground beef in place of the sirloin and skip the slicing.
steps.narration: If you want this quicker next time, swap in ground beef so there is no steak to slice.

ingredients.name: lo mein noodles or pad thai rice noodles

steps.text: Set out and prepare all the vegetables before any heat goes on.
steps.narration: Start by getting the carrots, broccoli, green onions and cabbage cut and within reach.

detail.how: This dish moves fast once the pan is hot, so every vegetable needs to be cut and sitting in a bowl before you begin. Line the bowls up in the order they go into the skillet.
detail.watch_for: Chopping while the pan is already going. Something always scorches while your back is turned.

steps.text: Split one bunch of green onions, cutting the tops into 1 in lengths and the whites into thin slices.
steps.narration: Separate the green tops from the white bottoms. Cut the tops into inch-long pieces and slice the whites thinly.

detail.how: The white bottoms are firmer and go in early with the other hard vegetables, while the green tops are delicate and are stirred in right at the end. Keeping them in two piles saves you sorting through a single heap later.
detail.watch_for: Tossing everything in at once, which turns the green tops slimy and dull.

steps.text: Cut 8 oz (227 g) of broccoli into bite-sized pieces.
steps.narration: Cut the broccoli down into pieces you can eat in one bite.

detail.how: Baby broccoli works well here and its stems are tender enough to use, so cut them up along with the tops. Regular broccoli is a fine swap, though the thick stalks on those are worth trimming away.
detail.watch_for: Leaving florets too large. Big pieces stay raw in the middle during a short stir fry.

steps.text: Peel 1/4 lb (113 g) of carrots into long thin ribbons.
steps.narration: Run a vegetable peeler down the length of the carrots to make ribbons.

detail.how: Lay the carrot flat on the board and drag the peeler from end to end, rotating as you go. Ribbons this thin are cooked through almost the moment they hit the pan, so you never end up chewing a hard chunk of raw carrot.
detail.watch_for: A dull peeler. It tears the carrot instead of shaving it and makes the job miserable.

steps.text: Mince 4 cloves (20 g) of garlic and measure out 2 cups (180 g) of shredded cabbage.
steps.narration: Mince the garlic, then weigh out the shredded cabbage.

detail.how: A bagged coleslaw mix is a reasonable shortcut if you do not want a whole head of cabbage sitting in the fridge. Set the garlic aside on its own, since it goes in near the very end rather than with the vegetables.
detail.watch_for: Adding the garlic early with the other aromatics, where it burns before the dish is done.

steps.text: Soak 8 oz (227 g) of noodles in boiling water until softened, or cook them as the package directs.
steps.narration: Cover the noodles with boiling water and let them soften while you cook everything else.

detail.how: Rice noodles only need a soak in very hot water, so set the bowl aside and leave them alone. Do not pour that water away later, because half a cup of it goes into the sauce and its starch is what makes the sauce cling.
detail.watch_for: Over-soaking. Noodles that are already fully soft will break apart when you stir them into the skillet.
detail.duration_hint: Roughly the time it takes to cook the beef.

steps.text: Heat your largest skillet over high heat, add 2 tbsp (30 g) of oil, then 2 lb (908 g) of ground beef.
steps.narration: Get the biggest pan you own screaming hot, add the oil, then the beef.

detail.how: Everything in this recipe eventually shares one pan, so pick the widest one in the cupboard. Extra lean beef gives the highest protein per serving, but a fattier grind or ground turkey both work.
detail.watch_for: Using a small skillet. A crowded pan drops in temperature and the beef stews in its own liquid.

steps.text: Spread the beef flat, salt it, poke a few holes for steam, and let it brown undisturbed.
steps.narration: Press the beef into an even layer, season it with salt and leave it alone for a few minutes.

detail.how: Push the meat out so it covers the whole base of the pan, then open a few gaps in it so the steam has somewhere to go instead of pooling underneath. Leave it still until the underside has taken on colour.
detail.watch_for: Breaking it up straight away. Meat that is stirred constantly releases water and turns grey.
detail.duration_hint: A few minutes before the first stir.

steps.text: Season the beef with 1 tsp (3 g) of white pepper and 2 tsp (6 g) of paprika, and stir to coat.
steps.narration: Add the white pepper and paprika, then stir them through the meat.

detail.how: Dropping dry spices onto the hot surface of the pan for a moment wakes up their aroma before they mix into the meat. Keep the beef moving once the spices are in so nothing sits on bare metal and scorches.
detail.watch_for: Letting the paprika sit on the hot pan too long, where it turns bitter fast.

steps.text: Keep smashing the beef until it is in tiny pebble-sized pieces and cooked through.
steps.narration: Work the beef down into very small crumbles as it finishes cooking.

detail.how: Press down with the edge of a wooden spoon or a potato masher rather than just stirring. Fine crumbles catch the sauce far better than chunks and are much easier to eat out of a container with a fork.
detail.watch_for: Leaving big lumps. They stay dry inside and never pick up any sauce.

steps.text: Transfer the cooked beef to a plate and set it aside.
steps.narration: Scoop the beef out of the skillet onto a plate so the pan is free for the vegetables.

steps.text: Add 1 tbsp (15 g) more oil to the skillet, then the broccoli, green onion whites and carrot ribbons.
steps.narration: Pour a little more oil into the hot pan and tip in the broccoli, onion whites and carrots.

detail.how: Toss the vegetables so they all pick up a film of oil, which is what carries the heat into them and helps them colour. The pan should still be hot from the beef, so they will start sizzling immediately.
detail.watch_for: Adding the delicate green tops now. Those wait until the end.
detail.duration_hint: One or two minutes before the cabbage joins them.

steps.text: Add 2 cups (180 g) of shredded cabbage to the pan.
steps.narration: Tip in the shredded cabbage once the other vegetables have had a minute or two.

detail.how: Cabbage looks like a huge pile going in and collapses to almost nothing, so do not be alarmed by the volume. It bulks the finished portions up without contributing many calories or a strong flavour of its own.
detail.watch_for: Expecting it to stay crunchy. Cabbage gives up water and shrinks by more than half.

steps.text: Cook the vegetables 3 to 5 minutes until softened and lightly charred, then slide the pan aside.
steps.narration: Keep the vegetables moving for a few minutes until they soften and pick up some char, then move the pan off the heat.

detail.how: You are after colour on the edges, not full tenderness, since these get reheated in a microwave later in the week. Pull the pan off the burner while you mix the sauce so nothing overcooks while your attention is elsewhere.
detail.watch_for: Cooking them until fully soft now. They will be mushy by the time you eat them.

steps.text: Mix 3 tbsp (45 g) soy sauce, 3 tbsp (45 g) oyster sauce, 2 tbsp (30 g) gochujang and 1/2 cup (120 g) of the hot noodle water in a bowl.
steps.narration: Combine the soy sauce, oyster sauce, gochujang and half a cup of the noodle soaking water.

detail.how: Stir the noodles around in their bowl first so the starch clouds the water, then dip a cup in and lift out half a cup of it. That starch is what thickens the sauce enough to coat the noodles instead of pooling at the bottom of the pan.
detail.watch_for: Using plain water. Without the starch the sauce stays thin and slides straight off.

steps.text: Stir 2 tbsp (42 g) of honey into the sauce until it dissolves.
steps.narration: Add the honey and stir the sauce until it is smooth.

steps.text: Return the beef to the skillet, add the soaked noodles, then pour the sauce over and fold gently.
steps.narration: Put the beef back in, lift the noodles straight out of their bowl into the pan, stir the sauce once more and pour it over.

detail.how: Give the sauce a final stir before it goes in, since the honey and gochujang settle at the bottom. Fold with a lifting motion from underneath rather than dragging a spoon through, and keep going until the noodles have taken on the colour of the sauce.
detail.watch_for: Stirring roughly. Soaked rice noodles snap easily into short useless pieces.

steps.text: Stir in the minced garlic and the green onion tops and cook 1 to 2 minutes.
steps.narration: Add the garlic and the green onion tops last and give them a minute or two in the heat.

detail.how: Going in at the very end means the garlic loses its raw bite without ever browning, and the onion tops keep their colour and freshness. A minute or two is genuinely all they need.
detail.watch_for: Leaving them in longer. Burnt garlic will make the whole batch taste acrid all week.

steps.text: Taste, adjust with salt and pepper, then divide the skillet evenly between five containers.
steps.narration: Taste it, correct the seasoning, then split everything between five meal prep containers.

detail.how: Season now rather than later, because a container of noodles is awkward to fix once it is cold. Weigh the full pan and divide by five if you want the portions truly identical.
detail.watch_for: Under-salting. The sauce tastes noticeably flatter after a night in the fridge.

steps.text: For extra smokiness, sear over the highest heat your carbon steel or cast iron pan will hold.
steps.narration: If you can get a heavy pan truly ripping hot, you will pick up some of that smoky stir fry character.

detail.how: That savoury smoke comes from food searing at temperatures a home burner struggles to reach. A heavy carbon steel or cast iron pan holds heat far better than thin nonstick, so preheat it long and hard and cook in smaller batches.
detail.watch_for: Chasing this with a light nonstick pan. It will not hold the heat and the coating suffers.

steps.text: Tuck a lemon wedge into each container as an optional garnish.
steps.narration: Add a wedge of lemon to each container if you like.

detail.how: A squeeze of lemon after the meal comes out of the microwave lifts the whole bowl and cuts through the richness of the sauce. Squeeze it at the table, not before storing.
detail.watch_for: Juicing it in advance, which dulls both the noodles and the brightness you were after.

steps.text: Let the containers cool, put the lids on and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Leave them open until they cool, then lid them and move them into the fridge for the week.

detail.how: Sealing warm food traps steam that drips back onto the noodles and turns them soggy. Once cold, lid them and they hold for five days; reheat in the microwave and finish with the lemon.
detail.watch_for: Lidding them hot. It is the fastest way to ruin the texture of the noodles.

steps.text: Cook 2 cups (300 g) of rice.
steps.narration: Get the rice going first so it is ready when you need it.

detail.how: Cook it however you normally do, and consider making a larger batch than the recipe calls for. Cooked rice sitting in the fridge is useful all week and costs nothing extra to make now.
detail.watch_for: Waiting until the end to start it. Rice takes longer than anything else here.

steps.text: In a bowl on a scale, combine 3 tbsp (45 g) lime juice, 3 tbsp (45 g) sriracha, 2 1/2 tbsp (50 g) honey, 2 tsp (6 g) garlic powder, 2 tsp (6 g) onion powder, 1 tsp (6 g) salt and 1 tsp (3 g) black pepper.
steps.narration: Build the sauce in one bowl set on a scale, adding each ingredient in turn.

detail.how: Sitting the bowl on a scale and zeroing between additions means you never dirty a measuring spoon. This one batch of sauce does double duty: half marinates the chicken and half dresses the finished bowls.
detail.watch_for: Forgetting to zero the scale between ingredients.

steps.text: Whisk the sauce until the seasonings are fully incorporated, adding a tablespoon of oil if you like.
steps.narration: Whisk everything together until smooth. A spoonful of oil is a nice extra if the calories are not a concern.

detail.how: Honey sinks and clings to the bottom of the bowl, so keep whisking past the point where it looks mixed. The powdered garlic and onion also need working in or they sit on the surface as dry clumps.
detail.watch_for: Streaks of unmixed honey, which mean some pieces of chicken get all the sweetness.

steps.text: Trim 2 lb (908 g) of chicken thighs, pour over half the sauce and mix with your hands.
steps.narration: Trim the fat off the thighs, add half the sauce and work it in by hand.

detail.how: Cut away loose fat and any skin left behind, then use your hands rather than a spoon so the marinade reaches into every fold of the meat. Keep the other half of the sauce covered and set aside for the end.
detail.watch_for: Using the whole batch of sauce now. Half of it belongs in the skillet later.

steps.text: Line a large sheet tray with foil and spray it lightly with oil.
steps.narration: Cover a big sheet tray with foil and give it a light coat of oil.

detail.how: The sauce has honey in it and will weld itself to a bare pan, so the foil is worth the trouble for cleanup alone. Letting the chicken marinate an hour or two in the fridge improves it, but cooking right away works fine.
detail.watch_for: Skipping the oil on the foil. Sugary marinade sticks to foil too.

steps.text: Lay the thighs smooth side down with space between them and bake at 400F / 204C for about 30 minutes.
steps.narration: Arrange the chicken on the tray, smooth side down and well spaced, then put it in a 400F / 204C oven for around 30 minutes.

detail.how: Gaps between the pieces let hot air circulate so the thighs roast rather than steam. Use two trays if one is not big enough to give every piece room.
detail.watch_for: Crowding the tray. Pieces that touch stay pale and wet where they meet.

steps.text: Weigh out 400 g of Japanese sweet potato, or any sweet potato you can find.
steps.narration: You need two small or one large Japanese sweet potato, about 400 g worth.

detail.how: Japanese sweet potatoes are drier and firmer than the orange kind, which is why they hold up so well in a reheated bowl. They can be hard to track down, so any variety substitutes without changing the method.
detail.watch_for: Nothing much. Swap freely if your shop does not stock them.

steps.text: Cut the sweet potato into a large dice of roughly 1/2 in cubes, then halve 4 to 5 green onions to separate tops from bottoms.
steps.narration: Chop the potato into half-inch cubes, then cut the green onions in half so the tops and the whites are apart.

detail.how: Aim for cubes of a consistent size so they finish roasting at the same moment. Later the chicken gets cut to roughly this same size, which is what makes the finished bowl eat evenly.
detail.watch_for: Mixed sizes. Small cubes burn while the large ones are still hard.

steps.text: Wash the green onions thoroughly to get the grit out from between the layers.
steps.narration: Rinse the green onions properly, because dirt hides down inside the layers.

detail.how: Soil packs into the tight layers near the root end and survives a quick rinse under the tap. Fan the layers apart with your fingers under running water and check the pieces again after you cut them.
detail.watch_for: A single rinse. You will find grit later, in the finished meal.

steps.text: Slice the green onions thinly, keeping whites and tops separate, then toss the potato with 1 tbsp (15 g) olive oil, salt and pepper.
steps.narration: Slice the onions thin in two separate piles, then coat the diced potato in olive oil, salt and pepper.

detail.how: The whites get cooked with the broccoli, while the green tops are scattered over the finished bowls, so they never end up back in the same pile. Toss the potato in a big bowl so every cut face picks up oil.
detail.watch_for: Skimping on the oil. Dry patches of potato stick to the tray and stay leathery.

steps.text: Spread the potato on a sheet tray and roast at 400F / 204C for 20 to 25 minutes.
steps.narration: Tip the potato onto a tray in one layer and slide it into the same oven as the chicken for 20 to 25 minutes.

detail.how: It shares the oven with the chicken, so give each tray its own rack rather than stacking food. If you would rather skip cooking rice altogether, double the potato and use it as the whole starch.
detail.watch_for: Heaping the cubes. Piled potato steams itself soft instead of browning.

steps.text: Thaw the frozen broccoli in the microwave at 50% power for a few minutes and drain off the water.
steps.narration: Defrost the broccoli in the microwave on half power, then pour away the liquid it releases.

detail.how: The aim is only to take the freeze out of it, not to cook it, so half power and a few minutes is enough. Draining the melted ice matters because that water would otherwise boil in the skillet and stop the broccoli browning.
detail.watch_for: Full power. It cooks the florets to mush before they ever reach the pan.

steps.text: Toss the broccoli with the scallion whites, 1 tbsp (15 g) oil, salt and pepper, and set it aside.
steps.narration: Put the thawed broccoli into the same bowl you used for the potato, add the onion whites, oil and seasoning, and mix.

steps.text: At the 20 to 25 minute mark, flip the chicken and turn the potatoes, then return both for 5 to 10 minutes.
steps.narration: Pull both trays out, turn the chicken over and stir the potatoes around, then send them back in for another 5 to 10 minutes.

detail.how: Turning the thighs lets the second side pick up the same colour the first one got sitting against the hot tray. The potato cubes need the same treatment so they brown on more than one face.
detail.watch_for: Leaving them untouched the whole time, which gives you one browned side and one pale one.

steps.text: Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat and add the broccoli and scallion whites.
steps.narration: While the trays finish, get a large skillet hot and add the broccoli and onion whites.

detail.how: You want colour on the florets and a little flavour built into them, not tenderness. Spread them out and let them sit against the pan before you start stirring.
detail.watch_for: Constant stirring, which keeps the surface too cool for any browning.

steps.text: Cook the broccoli only 3 to 5 minutes, stopping while it is still slightly underdone.
steps.narration: Give it three to five minutes and leave it a little firmer than you would normally serve it.

detail.how: Reheating in the microwave later is effectively a second round of cooking, so anything you cook fully now will be overcooked when you actually eat it. Deliberately stopping short is what keeps the texture good on day four.
detail.watch_for: Cooking to perfect doneness now. It will be soft and grey by the time it is lunch.

steps.text: Rest the roasted chicken, then cut it into a medium to large dice matching the potato cubes.
steps.narration: Take the chicken out, let it rest a few minutes, then chop it into pieces about the size of the potato cubes.

detail.how: Resting lets the juices settle so they stay in the meat rather than running out across your board. Matching the potato size means every forkful of the finished bowl carries a bit of each component.
detail.watch_for: Cutting it straight from the oven, which loses the juices and leaves the chicken dry.

steps.text: Return the skillet to medium heat, add the chicken and sweet potato, then stir in the remaining sauce.
steps.narration: Put the pan back on medium, add the chicken and potatoes, mix, then pour in the rest of the sauce.

detail.how: There is a lot of food at this point, so use the biggest skillet you own or the mixing turns into a wrestling match. Stir until the sauce has coated everything evenly rather than sitting in one corner.
detail.watch_for: A pan that is too small. Food goes over the sides and the sauce never distributes.

steps.text: Add the 2 cups (300 g) of cooked rice last and stir it through.
steps.narration: Now tip the rice in and stir it into everything else.

detail.how: The rice waits until after the sauce is in for a reason: dry grains soak up liquid greedily and would take the sauce away from the chicken and vegetables. Coating everything else first means the rice only picks up what is left over.
detail.watch_for: Adding rice before the sauce, which leaves the chicken bland and the rice soggy.

steps.text: Taste, adjust with salt and pepper, then divide the skillet between five containers.
steps.narration: Have a taste, fix the seasoning, and share the contents of the pan across five meal prep containers.

steps.text: Eyeball the portions, or weigh the total and divide by five for exact ones.
steps.narration: Scooping by eye is fine if you are eating all five yourself. For exact portions, weigh the lot and divide by five.

detail.how: Any difference between containers averages out over a week if the same person eats them all. If you want them identical, put the empty container on a scale, note its weight, and fill each to the same target.
detail.watch_for: Overfilling the first two containers and coming up short on the last.

steps.text: Top each bowl with green onion tops and a lime wedge, then cool, lid and refrigerate up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Scatter the green onion tops over and add a lime wedge to each, then let them cool before lidding and refrigerating.

detail.how: Leave the lids off until the containers are no longer warm, otherwise steam condenses and pools under the rice. Once cold they hold for five days.
detail.watch_for: Sealing them while hot, which waterlogs the rice by the next morning.

steps.text: To reheat, lift out the lime, microwave about 2 minutes, then squeeze the lime over and stir.
steps.narration: Take the lime wedge out first, microwave for roughly two minutes, then squeeze the lime in and mix it through.

detail.how: The lime goes in after heating, not before, so its brightness survives. Stirring once it is out of the microwave spreads both the juice and the heat evenly through the bowl.
detail.watch_for: Microwaving the lime wedge along with the food.

ingredients.name: top round steak, also sold as London broil
bell peppers, one red and one green

steps.text: Have 4 cups (600 g) of day old cooked rice ready.
steps.narration: This recipe wants four cups of cooked rice, ideally cooked the day before.

detail.how: Rice that has spent a night in the fridge has dried out slightly, so the grains stay separate in the pan rather than clumping into paste. Freshly cooked rice still works, it just gives a stickier result.
detail.watch_for: Hot, just cooked rice. Its surface moisture turns the whole pan gluey.
detail.duration_hint: Cook the rice a day ahead.

steps.text: In a bowl on a scale, mix 1 tbsp (15 g) oil, 1 tbsp (15 g) soy sauce and 1 tsp (3 g) each of garlic powder, onion powder, chili powder, paprika and black pepper.
steps.narration: Build the marinade in one bowl set on a scale: oil, soy sauce, then a teaspoon each of the five seasonings.

steps.text: Add 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and 1/2 tsp (2 g) baking soda, then mix and set the marinade aside.
steps.narration: Finish the marinade with the salt and the baking soda, stir it smooth and leave it while you cut the meat.
