detail.how: Baking soda raises the surface pH of the beef, which stops the proteins from tightening as hard when they hit the pan and leaves the meat noticeably more tender. Stir it through properly so no dry pockets are left sitting in the liquid.
detail.watch_for: Adding more than the recipe says. Too much baking soda leaves a soapy taste on the meat.

steps.text: Get 1 1/2 lb (681 g) of top round steak.
steps.narration: You need a pound and a half of top round, which some shops label London broil.

detail.how: It is one of the leanest and usually the cheapest cuts on the shelf, which is exactly why it suits a lower calorie meal prep. It is also tough, so the baking soda and the small cut size are what make it pleasant to eat.
detail.watch_for: Nothing yet. Sirloin is an upgrade if you want to spend more.

steps.text: Firm the steak up in the freezer for a couple of hours before cutting.
steps.narration: Put the steak in the freezer for a couple of hours so it stiffens.

detail.how: Partly frozen beef holds its shape against the knife instead of squashing and sliding, which makes thin even cuts far easier. You want it firm to the touch, not frozen solid.
detail.watch_for: Freezing it right through. A solid block cannot be cut safely.

steps.text: Plan to cut this lean beef small rather than into large pieces.
steps.narration: Because the cut is so lean, keep the pieces small.

detail.how: Big pieces of a lean, tough cut turn chewy no matter how carefully you cook them. Cutting it down into small bites shortens the muscle fibres so each piece gives way easily.
detail.watch_for: Treating this like a steak you would sear whole. It is not that cut.

steps.text: Slice the steak into 1/4 in strips, turn them 90 degrees and cut across into small pieces, then add it to the marinade.
steps.narration: Cut the beef into quarter-inch strips, turn them a quarter turn and cut across into small dice, then tip it into the bowl of marinade.

detail.how: Cutting in two passes at right angles gives you even cubes quickly without measuring anything. Get everything into the marinade bowl at once so no pieces are left dry.
detail.watch_for: Uneven pieces. The small ones overcook while the large ones stay tough.

steps.text: Mix the beef by hand until every piece is coated, squeezing it as you go.
steps.narration: Get your hands in and work the marinade over every piece, giving the meat a squeeze while you do it.

detail.how: Hands reach into the gaps a spoon cannot, and the squeezing itself breaks down some of the connective tissue in a tough cut. Be reasonably rough with it here.
detail.watch_for: Gently folding it with a spoon, which leaves dry pieces and skips the tenderising.

steps.text: Let the beef marinate for about an hour, or at least while you chop the vegetables.
steps.narration: An hour of marinating is ideal, though the time it takes to chop the vegetables will do.

detail.how: The baking soda needs contact time to work on the surface of the meat, so longer is genuinely better here. If you are in a hurry, chopping the vegetables buys you fifteen minutes for free.
detail.watch_for: Going straight from mixing to the pan, which wastes the tenderising step.

steps.text: Trim and seed 2 medium bell peppers of 150 g each, dice them to match the beef, then cut 1 small onion (100 g) into thin strips.
steps.narration: Cut the ends off the peppers, take out the seed cores and dice them to the size of the beef, then slice the onion into thin strips.

detail.how: Using one red and one green pepper gives the finished bowls some colour contrast. Cutting the onion into strips rather than dice gives you two different textures in the pan instead of one uniform one.
detail.watch_for: Dicing the peppers much larger than the beef, which makes the bowls eat unevenly.

steps.text: Smash 2 cloves (10 g) of garlic under the flat of your knife and mince them.
steps.narration: Crush the garlic cloves with the side of the knife, then chop them fine.

steps.text: Measure out 3 tbsp (45 g) of chipotle peppers and adobo sauce combined.
steps.narration: Weigh out three tablespoons of chipotles and their adobo sauce together.

detail.how: Chipotles are smoked, dried jalapenos, so they bring smoke as well as heat. The three tablespoons is a combined weight, which lets you shift the balance between pepper and sauce to suit how much heat you want.
detail.watch_for: Assuming this is mild. Whole chipotles carry a real kick.

steps.text: Press the peppers against the can with a spoon to squeeze out sauce for a milder result, then finely mince the two chipotles you use.
steps.narration: For flavour without much heat, press the peppers with a spoon to squeeze the sauce out of them, then chop the chipotles very fine.

detail.how: Most of the smoky flavour lives in the adobo sauce while most of the heat lives in the peppers themselves, so leaning on the sauce keeps the dish gentle. Two whole peppers plus enough sauce to reach 45 g is a good middle ground.
detail.watch_for: Large chunks of chipotle. Whoever bites into one gets the entire dish's heat at once.

steps.text: Heat a large skillet over medium heat with 1/2 tbsp (7.5 g) of oil and plan to cook the beef in two batches.
steps.narration: Set a large skillet over medium heat, about five out of ten, add half a tablespoon of oil, and cook the beef in two goes.

detail.how: Two batches keeps the pan from being overloaded, which would drop the temperature and leave the beef grey and wet. Splitting it costs a couple of extra minutes and buys you real browning.
detail.watch_for: Tipping all the beef in at once. It will steam rather than sear.

steps.text: Spread the first batch in one layer, leave it undisturbed 90 seconds, then turn it and cook the other side.
steps.narration: Get the beef into a single layer and leave it alone for about ninety seconds before turning it over.

detail.how: Pieces cut this small cook remarkably fast, roughly 90 seconds to 2 minutes a side. The stillness is what builds the crust, so resist stirring until the first side has set.
detail.watch_for: Stirring early. Nothing browns and the beef ends up boiled in its own juice.

steps.text: Move the first batch to a plate, add another 1/2 tbsp of oil and cook the rest of the beef.
steps.narration: Take the cooked beef out onto a plate, add a little more oil and repeat with the remaining beef.

steps.text: Transfer all the beef to the plate to rest while you cook the vegetables.
steps.narration: Once the second batch is done, put it with the first and let the meat rest.

detail.how: Cutting the beef before cooking feels like extra work, but it cooks so quickly that the total time comes out about the same as searing it whole. It is also more forgiving, which helps if you are still building confidence at the stove.
detail.watch_for: Discarding the juices that collect on the plate. They go back into the pan later.

steps.text: Add 2 tsp (10 g) of oil to the same pan and saute the onion and peppers for a few minutes to soften.
steps.narration: Into the same pan goes a little more oil, then the onions and peppers to soften.

detail.how: The pan still holds oil and browned bits from the beef, so it needs only a small top-up and the vegetables pick up all that flavour as they cook. Toss them to coat before you leave them to soften.
detail.watch_for: Washing the pan between steps and throwing away the best flavour in the dish.

steps.text: Add 1 cup (150 g) of frozen corn and the garlic, and cook another minute or two.
steps.narration: After a couple of minutes tip in the corn and scatter the garlic on top, then keep it moving for another minute or two.

detail.how: The corn goes straight in frozen and needs only enough time to heat through. Garlic comes in last because it burns quickly, and a minute in a hot pan is all it needs.
detail.watch_for: Adding the garlic with the onions at the start, where it scorches and turns bitter.

steps.text: Clear a well in the middle of the vegetables and add 4 cups (600 g) of day old rice.
steps.narration: Push the vegetables out to the sides to make a space in the centre and add the rice there.

detail.how: The well puts the rice in direct contact with the hot base of the pan so it warms and loosens quickly instead of sitting cold on top of the vegetables. For reference, 250 g of dry rice cooked the day before yields roughly this amount.
detail.watch_for: Dumping the rice over everything, which leaves cold clumps in the middle.

steps.text: Break up the rice clumps, then add 2 tbsp (30 g) soy sauce, 1 tbsp (15 g) lime juice and the 3 tbsp (45 g) of chopped chipotles.
steps.narration: Work the clumps of rice apart, then pour in the soy sauce, the lime juice and the chopped chipotles with their sauce.

detail.how: Press the clumps against the pan with the back of your spoon until the grains separate, otherwise the seasoning coats only the outside of each lump. Add the liquids once the rice is loose so they spread evenly.
detail.watch_for: Seasoning clumped rice. The inside stays plain and pale.

steps.text: Stir thoroughly, add the beef with all its resting juices, stir again and taste for salt and pepper.
steps.narration: Mix everything until the rice is evenly coloured, return the beef along with the juices on the plate, stir once more and taste.

detail.how: Keep mixing until there is no white rice left showing, so the chipotle, soy and lime are spread through the whole pan. Everything that pooled on the plate under the beef is concentrated flavour, so scrape it in.
detail.watch_for: Adding the beef too early. It sits over heat longer than it needs and toughens.

steps.text: Divide the skillet evenly between five meal prep containers.
steps.narration: Line up five containers and split the pan between them.

steps.text: Swap in ground beef, or step up to sirloin, if you prefer.
steps.narration: Ground beef works as a substitute here, and sirloin is an upgrade if you do not mind the cost.

detail.how: Steak gives a meatier flavour and a chewier texture than ground beef, which is worth having as a change in a meal prep rotation. Sirloin tastes better still, but costs more and is slightly less lean than top round.
detail.watch_for: Nothing critical. All three cuts work with this method.

steps.text: Garnish each container with lime wedges and chopped cilantro.
steps.narration: Finish each meal with a lime wedge and a scattering of cilantro, both optional.

steps.text: For more protein, raise the steak to 2 lb.
steps.narration: Using two pounds of steak instead pushes each serving to around 48 g of protein.

detail.how: At 1 1/2 lb each portion lands near 497 calories with 38 g of protein, which is what keeps it under the 500 mark. Going to 2 lb brings it to roughly 48 g of protein per serving at a higher calorie count.
detail.watch_for: Overloading the pan. More meat means an extra batch when browning.

steps.text: Let the containers cool, put the lids on and refrigerate for up to five days.
steps.narration: Once they have cooled, lid them and move them into the fridge for the week.

detail.how: Waiting until they are cool keeps steam from condensing under the lid and softening the rice. They keep for five days in the fridge.
detail.watch_for: Sealing them warm, which leaves the rice wet and sticky.

ingredients.name: bell peppers, one red and one green

steps.text: Cook enough rice to yield 3 cups (450 g) cooked.
steps.narration: Get the rice going first so it is ready when everything else lands.

detail.how: The rice is here mainly to carry calories, so measure by the cooked weight rather than the dry. Start it before any knife work and it will finish on its own while you handle the potatoes and beef.
detail.watch_for: Cooking too little. Extra cooked rice keeps fine and turns into fried rice later in the week.

steps.text: Scrub 3 1/3 lb (1.5 kg) of russet potatoes.
steps.narration: Weigh out about three and a third pounds of russets, roughly nine small to medium potatoes.

steps.text: Cut the potatoes into a large dice.
steps.narration: Chop the potatoes into big even cubes.

detail.how: Any shape roasts fine here, but chunks are the easiest to move around a hot sheet pan since you can just shake the tray instead of turning pieces one by one. Keep the cubes close to the same size so they finish together.
detail.watch_for: Mixing tiny scraps with large chunks. The small pieces will be burnt by the time the big ones soften.

steps.text: Season the potatoes with 2 tbsp (30 g) oil, 1 tsp (6 g) salt, 2 tsp (6 g) black pepper and 2 tsp (6 g) garlic powder.
steps.narration: Set a large bowl on a scale, add the potatoes and weigh in the oil and seasonings.

detail.how: Weighing straight into the bowl on a scale keeps the oil accounted for in the macros and saves washing extra cups. The seasoning list is a starting point only, so swap in whatever flavour direction you want.
detail.watch_for: Skimping on oil. Dry potatoes stick to the pan and never crisp.

steps.text: Toss the potatoes until coated, then oil two sheet pans.
steps.narration: Stir and shake the potatoes until every piece is slick, then spray your trays.

steps.text: Spread the potatoes across both pans and roast at 400F / 204C for 25 minutes.
steps.narration: Split the potatoes between two trays so they are not piled up, then get them into the oven.

detail.how: Two pans is the whole point at this volume. Potatoes packed tight trap their own steam and come out pale and soft instead of browned. Give each cube a little bare pan around it.
detail.watch_for: Crowding one tray to save washing up. You lose all the browning that carries this dish.
detail.duration_hint: About 25 minutes, turned at the halfway point.

steps.text: Cut 250 g of bell peppers into thin strips about 1 inch long.
steps.narration: Slice the peppers into short thin strips.

detail.how: Strips keep a bit of bite in the finished bowl, which is what makes it read as a cheesesteak. One red and one green pepper gives some colour contrast against all the beige. Dice them instead if you would rather they disappear into the mix.
detail.watch_for: Cutting them thick. Chunky peppers stay crunchy and stand apart from the sauce.

steps.text: Slice half an onion into matching strips and mince 3 cloves of garlic.
steps.narration: Cut the onion the same size as the peppers, then mince the garlic.

detail.how: Match the onion strips to the pepper strips so both soften at the same rate in the pan. The garlic is 15 g total and goes in much later than the other two, so keep it in its own pile.
detail.watch_for: Mincing the garlic and tossing it in with the peppers. It burns long before the peppers are done.

steps.text: Pull both trays at the 15 minute mark and toss the potatoes.
steps.narration: Take the trays out partway through and shake the potatoes around.

detail.how: Swap the trays between racks while you are at it. The upper tray sits in the steam rising off the lower one and browns noticeably slower, so it will want a few extra minutes at the end.
detail.watch_for: Assuming both trays are done at the same time. Judge each one by colour, not the clock.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp (15 g) oil in a large skillet over medium-high and add 2 lb (908 g) of 90/10 ground beef.
steps.narration: Get a big skillet hot with a spoon of oil, then lay the beef in.

steps.text: Press the beef flat and let it sear undisturbed.
steps.narration: Spread the beef across the whole pan and leave it alone to build a crust.

detail.how: Flattening the beef puts the most surface possible against hot metal, and leaving it still is what lets that surface actually brown. Cooking in two batches would brown it better still, at the cost of extra time.
detail.watch_for: Breaking it up right away. Constantly stirred beef weeps water and turns grey instead of crusty.
detail.duration_hint: A few minutes before the first turn.

steps.text: Flip the beef and break it into smaller pieces as it cooks.
steps.narration: Turn the beef over, then start chopping it apart with your spoon.

steps.text: Move the beef to a plate at about 90 percent cooked, and pull the potatoes from the oven.
steps.narration: Once the beef is nearly done, transfer it out of the pan and set the roasted potatoes aside to cool.

detail.how: Leaving the beef slightly under means it will not turn dry when it goes back into the sauce later. Park the potato trays on the stovetop so they cool and firm up rather than steaming under a lid.
detail.watch_for: Cooking the beef all the way through now, then heating it again in the sauce and drying it out.

steps.text: Return the skillet to the heat with 1 tbsp (15 g) oil and cook the peppers and onions with a little salt.
steps.narration: Add more oil to the same pan and cook the peppers and onions with a pinch of salt.

detail.how: Tip the cut vegetables into the bowl the potatoes were seasoned in first so they pick up whatever oil is left clinging to it. Then let them sit over the heat long enough to take on some colour.
detail.watch_for: Overcooking them. The longer they go the softer they get, so pull back on the time if you want them to keep some structure.

steps.text: Stir in the garlic, cook one more minute, then take the pan off the heat.
steps.narration: Add the garlic at the end and give it a minute before pulling the pan.

steps.text: Combine 1 cup (240 g) beef broth, 1/4 cup (60 g) ketchup, 1 1/2 tbsp (23 g) worcestershire sauce, 1 tbsp (15 g) dijon mustard and 1 tbsp (8 g) cornstarch.
steps.narration: Build the sauce in a bowl while the vegetables cook.

steps.text: Whisk the sauce hard until no cornstarch is left sitting in it.
steps.narration: Whisk firmly so the cornstarch fully dissolves into the liquid.

detail.how: Cornstarch sinks and clumps, so keep whisking until the mixture looks uniform with no white streaks against the side of the bowl. It will settle again while it waits, which is why you whisk it a second time right before it goes in the pan.
detail.watch_for: Lumps of dry starch that never break down and end up as gummy spots in the sauce.

steps.text: Turn the heat to medium, add 3 cups (450 g) cooked rice and the beef, and stir to distribute.
steps.narration: Everything goes back in the pan now, rice and beef together.

detail.how: Work the spoon through the rice to break apart any clumps that formed as it cooled, so each bite gets the same mix of rice, beef and vegetables. If your skillet cannot hold all of it, shift the lot into a deep pot.
detail.watch_for: Cold rice packed into lumps. Those pockets stay bland because no sauce reaches inside them.

steps.text: Pour in the sauce, stir until thickened, then taste and season.
steps.narration: Whisk the sauce once more, pour it over and stir it through, then check the seasoning.

detail.how: The cornstarch does its work almost immediately, so by the time the sauce has reached every corner of the pan it is usually done. Then taste: the rice went in completely unseasoned, so it will pull salt out of the sauce.
detail.watch_for: Skipping the taste. A small amount of salt and pepper is nearly always needed at this point.

steps.text: Divide the beef mixture between five containers, push it to one side, and add the potatoes.
steps.narration: Portion the beef into five containers, shove it over, and fill the gap with potatoes.

detail.how: Keeping the potatoes in their own section rather than buried in the sauce matters, because you will want to reheat them separately to get the crisp back. Eyeballing five even portions is close enough unless you are tracking precisely.
detail.watch_for: Overfilling the first containers and coming up short on the last two.

steps.text: Lay two slices of provolone over each container.
steps.narration: Top every bowl with two slices of provolone, ten slices in total.

steps.text: Scatter chopped parsley over the top.
steps.narration: Finish with a little parsley for colour and freshness.

steps.text: Cool the containers, lid them and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Let everything cool before the lids go on, then store them in the fridge.

detail.how: Wait until the food is no longer throwing off steam before sealing, or the trapped moisture will drip back onto the potatoes and soften them. Each portion lands near 1,026 calories and 59 g of protein, counting 2 tbsp (30 g) of ketchup on the side for dipping.
detail.watch_for: Lidding while hot. That is what turns crisp roasted potatoes into damp ones by day two.

steps.text: Reheat the potatoes in an air fryer at 400F for about 5 minutes and the rest in the microwave for 2 minutes.
steps.narration: Crisp the potatoes in the air fryer or oven while the beef and rice go in the microwave.

detail.how: Run the air fryer first and start the microwave partway through so both parts finish together. Microwave the beef and rice for roughly 2 minutes, or until steaming through.
detail.watch_for: Microwaving the potatoes. They will taste fine but lose the crisp exterior entirely, which is the main reason to keep them separate in the container.
detail.duration_hint: About 5 minutes for the potatoes, 2 for the rest.

title: Chili Lime Chicken with Golden Rice

ingredients.name: small dried noodles, or spaghetti broken into 1/2 inch pieces

steps.text: Find small short noodles for the rice blend.
steps.narration: Track down the tiny pasta pieces that go into this style of rice.

detail.how: Many stores stock them ready cut. If they are not shelved with the other pasta, check the Latin foods aisle, where they often sit as fideo. Anyone avoiding gluten will likely need to break down a gluten-free pasta instead.
detail.watch_for: Assuming you have to buy a boxed rice mix. The whole point is that you are building it from scratch.

steps.text: Break 3 1/2 oz (100 g) of dried spaghetti into 1/2 inch pieces.
steps.narration: Snap the spaghetti into half inch lengths until you have a hundred grams.

detail.how: Hold a small bundle at a time and snap it over the bowl so the pieces do not scatter. They do not need to be identical, just short enough to sit alongside grains of rice.
detail.watch_for: Leaving long shards. Anything much over half an inch tangles instead of blending into the rice.

steps.text: Melt 2 tbsp (28 g) butter in a lidded pot over medium heat and toast the noodles in it.
steps.narration: Melt the butter in your best rice pot, then stir the broken noodles through it.

detail.how: Use the pot with the tightest fitting lid you own, since the rice will steam in it later. Stir the noodles so every piece is buttered, and expect them to puff slightly before they start taking on colour.
detail.watch_for: Walking away. Butter and small pasta pieces go from toasted to scorched quickly.

steps.text: Measure 1 tsp (3 g) onion powder, 1 tsp (3 g) garlic powder, 1/4 tsp (1 g) turmeric and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt into a small bowl.
steps.narration: While the noodles toast, gather the rice seasonings in one small bowl.

steps.text: When the noodles have browned after 3 to 4 minutes, add 1 cup (180 g) dry rice and the seasonings.
steps.narration: Once the noodles have changed colour and texture, tip in the rice and the spice bowl.

detail.how: You are looking for a shift from pale and glossy to a light golden tan across most of the pieces. That colour is a real flavour layer, so do not rush past it, but do not chase dark brown either.
detail.watch_for: Adding the rice too early. Untoasted noodles leave the dish tasting flat compared to the boxed version.

steps.text: Stir constantly for a minute or two so the rice coats in butter and the spices bloom.
steps.narration: Keep everything moving so the rice picks up the butter and the spices warm through.

detail.how: Dry spices hitting hot fat release far more aroma than they do sitting in liquid, but they also scorch in seconds. Constant motion is what keeps them on the right side of that line.
detail.watch_for: Letting the pot sit still. Turmeric in particular turns bitter the moment it burns.

steps.text: Pour in 2 cups (480 g) chicken broth plus 1/3 cup (80 g) water, for 560 g of liquid.
steps.narration: Add the broth and top it up with water to reach 560 grams of total liquid.

detail.how: The total liquid is what matters, not the split. If you have enough broth on hand to cover all 560 g, use broth for the lot and skip the water. Bone broth adds roughly 19 g of protein across the batch.
detail.watch_for: Guessing the volume. Too little liquid and the grains stay hard, too much and you get porridge.

steps.text: Bring the pot to a full rolling boil and hold it there for 1 minute.
steps.narration: Take the liquid all the way to a hard boil and keep it boiling for a full minute.

detail.how: A rolling boil means the whole surface is churning, not a few bubbles rising in one corner. The rice needs that temperature to hydrate evenly, and one minute at it is the target.
detail.watch_for: Capping the pot and dropping to a simmer before the real boil arrives. That is exactly what produces rice that is mushy outside and crunchy in the middle.

steps.text: For a foolproof version, do the toasting in a skillet and finish the rice in a rice cooker.
steps.narration: If the stovetop method worries you, toast in a pan and let a rice cooker handle the cooking.

steps.text: Cover tightly, drop the heat to low and simmer for 18 minutes.
steps.narration: Lid on, heat down to low, and leave it for eighteen minutes.

detail.how: The lid has to seal well or the steam that cooks the top layer escapes. Once the lid is on, leave it on; lifting it to peek resets the steam every time.
detail.watch_for: A loose or vented lid. That is the second half of the hard-rice problem, after skipping the boil.

steps.text: In a large bowl, weigh 2 tbsp (30 g) lime juice, 1 1/2 tbsp (22.5 g) oil and 1 1/2 tsp (9 g) salt.
steps.narration: Set a big bowl on the scale and start the marinade with lime juice, oil and salt.

steps.text: Add 1 tsp (3 g) each of onion powder, garlic powder, chili powder and paprika plus 1 tsp (1 g) dried oregano, stir, then add 2 lb (908 g) chicken thighs.
steps.narration: Stir the spices into the liquid until combined, then drop in the chicken thighs.

detail.how: Mix the marinade fully before the chicken goes near it, so the salt and spices are already dispersed rather than clinging to whichever piece they land on first.
detail.watch_for: Dumping dry spices on top of raw chicken. You get patchy seasoning and bare spots.

steps.text: Coat every surface of the thighs, then lay them smooth side down on an oiled sheet tray.
steps.narration: Work the marinade over both sides and into the folds, then spread the thighs on a greased tray.

detail.how: Chicken thighs have loose flaps and crevices that hide from the marinade, so open them out and push the mixture into every gap. Placing them smooth side down puts the flattest face against the hot pan.
detail.watch_for: Overlapping pieces on the tray. Where they touch, they steam rather than roast.

steps.text: Bake the chicken at 400F / 204C for 20 to 25 minutes, and rest the finished rice off the heat for 10 minutes.
steps.narration: Chicken into the oven, and once the rice hits eighteen minutes take it off the burner to steam for another ten.

detail.how: The rice keeps cooking on residual steam after the burner is off, which is what evens out the last of the moisture. Leave the lid on for the whole rest.
detail.watch_for: Opening the rice pot as soon as the timer goes. The extra ten minutes covered is part of the cooking, not a pause.
detail.duration_hint: 20 to 25 minutes for the chicken, 10 minutes rest for the rice.

steps.text: Cut 1/2 lb (227 g) of broccolini, slicing the stems thin on a bias and the tops into bite-size chunks.
steps.narration: Slice the broccolini stems thinly at an angle and chop the florets into pieces you can eat in one go.

detail.how: Broccolini stems are far more tender than regular broccoli stalks, so there is no need to discard them. Cutting them at an angle exposes more surface and helps them cook at the same rate as the softer tops.
detail.watch_for: Leaving stems thick. They will still be raw when the florets are done.

steps.text: Steam the broccolini in the microwave with 40 g of water under a plate for about 90 seconds.
steps.narration: Put the broccolini in a microwave-safe dish with a splash of water, cover it with a plate, and microwave it for a minute and a half.

detail.how: A plate laid over the dish traps enough steam to cook the vegetable without any added oil, which keeps the meal lighter given the butter in the rice and the oil in the marinade. Times vary with microwave power, so check at 90 seconds.
detail.watch_for: Overshooting. Broccolini goes from bright and crisp to drab and floppy in about fifteen seconds.

steps.text: Drain the broccolini and dress it with 2 tsp (10 g) lemon juice, salt and pepper.
steps.narration: Pour off any standing water, then season the broccolini with lemon juice, salt and pepper and set it aside.

steps.text: Pour about 60 g of water around the baked chicken to lift the pan drippings into a sauce.
steps.narration: Splash water around each piece on the hot tray and let it sit for a few minutes.

detail.how: The marinade cooks onto the tray as concentrated browned bits. Water poured around the chicken loosens all of it back into a thin sauce that you would otherwise scrub down the sink. Give it a few minutes to do the work on its own.
detail.watch_for: Pouring water directly over the chicken instead of around it, which washes the crust off the meat.

steps.text: Pull the chicken apart by hand into bite-size pieces.
steps.narration: Tear the thighs into bite-size chunks with your hands, gloves on if you like.

detail.how: Hand-torn chicken has ragged edges that catch far more sauce than clean knife cuts do, and the texture is noticeably better in a reheated meal prep. Wait until the pieces are cool enough to handle comfortably.
detail.watch_for: Tearing it too fine. Bite-size, not shredded to threads.

steps.text: Toss the torn chicken through the pan sauce and taste for salt.
steps.narration: Roll the chicken around the tray so it soaks up all the liquid, then taste it.

steps.text: Uncover the rested rice, fluff it and taste.
steps.narration: Take the lid off, fork the rice loose and try a spoonful.

detail.how: All the liquid should be gone by now. Run a fork through in lifting strokes rather than stirring, which separates the grains without mashing them.
detail.watch_for: Standing liquid in the bottom of the pot, a sign the boil or the seal was not there.

steps.text: Stir a pinch of msg into the rice if you want the boxed-mix flavour.
steps.narration: Add msg if the rice tastes like it is missing a savoury edge. This part is optional.

steps.text: Divide the rice, chicken and broccolini evenly between five containers.
steps.narration: Line up five containers and split everything between them.

detail.how: Portioning by eye is accurate enough for most people. If you are tracking macros closely, weigh each component and divide the total by five instead.
detail.watch_for: Filling containers one at a time to the brim and running out before the fifth.

steps.text: Cool the containers fully, lid them and refrigerate for up to 5 days.
steps.narration: Wait until they stop steaming, put the lids on and move them to the fridge.

detail.how: Each portion comes to roughly 537 calories and 46 g of protein when the rice is cooked in bone broth, or about 42 g using ordinary chicken broth.
detail.watch_for: Sealing them while steam is still rising, which leaves condensation pooling on the food.

steps.text: Remember the two rice rules: a tight lid, and a full boil before covering.
steps.narration: If you make this again, the pot lid and the rolling boil are the two things worth getting right.

detail.how: Almost nothing else in this recipe can go badly wrong. There is barely any knife work beyond the broccolini, which takes two or three minutes. The rice is the only step with a real failure mode.
detail.watch_for: Cutting either corner. Testing this recipe without them produced rice that stayed hard in the centre.

steps.text: Add 1 1/4 lb (568 g) of boneless skinless chicken breasts to a large pot of boiling water.
steps.narration: Start by dropping the chicken breasts into a big pot of boiling water.

steps.text: Boil the chicken 15 to 20 minutes until cooked through, then move it to a large bowl.
steps.narration: Let the breasts cook until they hit temperature, then lift them into a bowl.

detail.how: Timing depends entirely on how thick the breasts are, so go by internal temperature rather than the clock. Boiling would normally cost you flavour, but these end up wrapped in a heavily seasoned dough, so plain cooked chicken is all you need here.
detail.watch_for: Pulling them early. Undercooked centres will not shred and cannot be fixed later in the dough.

steps.text: Shred the chicken into small pieces.
steps.narration: Break the cooked chicken down into small pieces.

detail.how: Two forks pulled in opposite directions will get you there with some effort. A stand mixer or hand mixer does the same job in a fraction of the time and with none of the work.
detail.watch_for: Trying to shred it straight out of the pot while it is scalding.

steps.text: Run the chicken in a stand mixer with the paddle for 30 seconds to a minute.
steps.narration: If you have a stand mixer, put the chicken in the bowl with the paddle and let it break the meat down.

detail.how: The paddle tears the breast apart evenly, and if you let it keep going it will also chop the strands down into short pieces on its own. Short pieces matter because these are small biscuits and long strands stick out of the sides.
detail.watch_for: Running it far past a minute, which turns the chicken to paste rather than shreds.

steps.text: If you shredded by hand, chop through the chicken a few times to shorten the strands.
steps.narration: Fork-shredded chicken needs a few passes with a knife to cut the long strands down.

steps.text: Set the chicken aside to cool, then dice about 6 green onions (100 g), greens and whites.
steps.narration: Leave the chicken to cool while you finely chop the green onions, using the whole stalk.

steps.text: Measure out 2 cups (227 g) of shredded cheddar.
steps.narration: Weigh out the cheddar, and plan to cut it shorter if it came from a bag.

detail.how: Bagged pre-shredded cheese comes in long strands that hang over the edge of a small biscuit and burn on the pan. Shorter pieces sit inside the dough and keep the outside of the biscuit clean.
detail.watch_for: Skipping this and ending up with lacy burnt cheese welded to your sheet pans.

steps.text: Pile the cheese onto the onions and rock a knife over both to break them down.
steps.narration: Tip the cheese onto the chopped onions and rock your knife back and forth through the pile.

steps.text: Check the sodium on your buffalo sauce and adjust the dough salt accordingly.
steps.narration: Look at the label on your hot sauce, because it is already carrying most of the salt in this recipe.

detail.how: The sauce used here lists 420 mg of sodium per serving, which is why the dough only gets a small amount of added salt. A milder or lower-sodium brand will leave the biscuits tasting flat unless you add more.
detail.watch_for: Following the salt quantity blindly with a different brand of sauce.

steps.text: Stir 1/2 cup (120 g) of buffalo sauce into the chicken.
steps.narration: Pour the buffalo sauce straight onto the chicken and mix it in.

detail.how: Saucing the chicken on its own, before it joins the dough, lets the unseasoned meat absorb as much of the flavour as it can. Mix until no dry-looking chicken is left.
detail.watch_for: Adding the sauce to the whole dough instead. The chicken stays bland and the heat spreads thin.

steps.text: Weigh 2 2/3 cups (320 g) of oat flour into a large bowl.
steps.narration: Put a big bowl on the scale and add the oat flour.

detail.how: Oat flour is nothing more than rolled oats blitzed in a blender until powdery, so you can make it yourself if you cannot buy it. Weigh rather than scoop, since the flour packs differently every time.
detail.watch_for: Under-blending homemade oat flour and leaving whole flakes, which give the biscuits a coarse texture.

steps.text: Whisk in 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt, 2 tbsp (16 g) garlic powder, 3 tbsp (4 g) dried parsley and 2 tsp (8 g) baking soda.
steps.narration: Add the seasonings and baking soda to the flour and whisk them through.

detail.how: Whisking the dry mix does two jobs: it breaks up clumps in the oat flour and spreads the baking soda evenly. Uneven soda leaves some biscuits with a soapy bite and others flat.
detail.watch_for: Stirring lazily. Baking soda is potent and needs to be genuinely dispersed.

steps.text: Beat 4 eggs, add them to the dry mix along with 2 2/3 cups (600 g) of 2% cottage cheese and the onions.
steps.narration: Whisk the eggs until the yolks and whites are one colour, then add them, the cottage cheese and the onions to the bowl.

steps.text: Add the cheddar and the buffalo chicken, then mix hard, scraping the bottom of the bowl.
steps.narration: In goes the cheese and the sauced chicken, then mix everything into a dough.

detail.how: This is a stiff, heavy mix, so use force and get right down to the base of the bowl. Dry oat flour hiding underneath will never hydrate and shows up as powdery pockets in the baked biscuits.
detail.watch_for: Stopping while streaks of dry flour are still visible.

steps.text: Oil several sheet pans, or line them with parchment paper.
steps.narration: Grease a few sheet pans generously, since this dough likes to stick.

steps.text: Scoop 1 oz (28 g) portions onto the pans with 2 inches between them and bake at 375F / 190C.
steps.narration: Use a one ounce cookie scoop to portion the dough, leaving two inches around each one, then get the tray into the oven.

detail.how: A spring-loaded scoop with a release lever is far faster than two spoons and gives you consistent sizes, which matters when everything has to bake for the same time. Fill a pan and send it straight to the oven rather than waiting to fill them all.
detail.watch_for: Crowding the tray. These spread a little and will fuse if they are closer than two inches.

steps.text: Bake 15 to 17 minutes, until the tops are golden brown.
steps.narration: Give them fifteen to seventeen minutes, or until the tops have taken on colour.

detail.how: The full batch runs to roughly 80 biscuits, which took four trays. Go by the colour of the tops rather than the timer, since the last trays go into a fully heated oven and can run faster.
detail.watch_for: Pulling them pale. Underbaked centres stay wet and gummy from the cottage cheese.

steps.text: Refrigerate any dough you cannot bake yet and work through it in rounds.
steps.narration: If you are short on trays, keep the rest of the dough in the fridge and bake it in batches.

detail.how: No oven fits four trays at once, so either scale the recipe down or park the bowl in the fridge and bake through it across the day as pans free up.
detail.watch_for: Leaving raw dough sitting at room temperature between batches.

steps.text: Pull each tray as it finishes.
steps.narration: Take each tray out when its time is up.

steps.text: Slide something with a thin sharp edge under the biscuits to release them.
steps.narration: Get a thin metal edge underneath each biscuit to lift it off the pan.

detail.how: A metal spatula is the natural tool, but a bench scraper works just as well. How stubborn they are varies pan to pan, and some trays will let you lift them off with your fingers.
detail.watch_for: Tearing the bottoms off with a flexible plastic turner on a sticky pan.

steps.text: Cool the biscuits on the counter.
steps.narration: Let them come down to room temperature on the counter.

steps.text: Plan on freezing the batch for long-term storage.
steps.narration: These are built for the freezer rather than the fridge.

detail.how: Each biscuit runs about 43 calories and 3.8 g of protein, so a snack of eight comes to roughly 345 calories and 31 g of protein. At 80 biscuits, that is around ten snacks worth, which is far more than a fridge shelf life would allow.
detail.watch_for: Leaving a whole batch in the fridge and losing half of it.

steps.text: Consolidate the cooled biscuits onto a small tray and flash freeze them uncovered until solid.
steps.narration: Gather them onto a tray that fits your freezer and freeze them uncovered until they are hard.

detail.how: Freezing them loose and uncovered first means they set as individual pieces instead of one welded block, and it lets them take the pressure of a vacuum sealer without being crushed.
detail.watch_for: Bagging them soft. Vacuum pressure will flatten unfrozen biscuits into a single mass.

steps.text: Fill vacuum bags with the frozen biscuits in a single layer.
steps.narration: Load the frozen biscuits into bags, keeping them one layer deep.

steps.text: Vacuum seal the bags to keep air and moisture out.
steps.narration: Seal the bags under vacuum so nothing dries out or picks up freezer burn.

detail.how: Removing the air is what prevents freezer burn and keeps them tasting fresh for months. Resealable vacuum bags let you open one, take a handful and pump the air back out.
detail.watch_for: Storing them in a loosely closed bag, which frosts them over within weeks.

steps.text: Close the zip top firmly, then pump out the air.
steps.narration: Press the zip closed all the way along before you use the pump.

steps.text: To reheat soft, microwave a handful on a plate for about a minute.
steps.narration: For a softer bread-like biscuit, put a few on a plate and microwave them until hot.

detail.how: About a minute is the starting point for a small handful straight from the freezer, but go by whether they are hot through. This is the quickest route and gives the softest texture.
detail.watch_for: Overloading the plate. A big pile heats unevenly, leaving cold centres.

steps.text: To reheat crisp, air fry them from frozen at 375F for 6 to 7 minutes.
steps.narration: Or go straight from the freezer into the air fryer for six or seven minutes.

detail.how: No thawing needed. If your air fryer runs hot and the outsides colour before the middles thaw, give them a short spell in the microwave first to take the chill off, then finish them in the air fryer.
detail.watch_for: A hot-running air fryer burning the edges while the centre is still frozen.
